speechtext:

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Transport. maintopic: ALLEGED INADEQUACY OF ARRANGEMENT FOR SHIPPING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first of all the construction of a vessel is not in substitution for the Malibu Princess but rather in place of the also "temporary" but not so temporary services of the Bella Bella along the coastline. speechtext: The House resumed, from Monday, December 6, consideration of the motion of Mr. Andras that Bill C-19, to amend or repeal certain statutes to enable restraint of government expenditures, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates; and the amendment thereto of Mr. Holmes (p. 1393).

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday evening I started my remarks on the bill before us. If I may summarize, yesterday I was simply pointing out that it is rather unfortunate that the government is suggesting that this bill is a key point in their restraint program. As I said yesterday, basically the bill is not needed in the sense that the government could restrain its expenditures without passage of this bill, and indeed many aspects of the bill are window-dressing, high profile items which undoubtedly the government feels gives them the excuse to create the impression in the land that somehow it is a restraint government. Yet we know that this
Restraint of Government Expenditures has been the biggest spending government this country has ever seen.
I say that in view of the fact that, as we know, the government now says that it will control its spending to $42,252 million this year. The government expects to get credit for holding that line, as government members say, but the fact is that they are already breaking their own guidelines. They indicated that they would not allow spending in this country to go up at a faster rate than the gross national product increase in the country. The GNP increase will be approximately 11 per cent, yet we find that, based on the estimate the government has already announced, government spending will increase by 14 per cent, a full 3 per cent faster rate of increase than that of the economy. Unfortunately, that will result in a greater government component in our GNP, which in turn puts more pressure than we have had until the present time on the average wage earner and taxpayer in this country.
This is why we want to emphasize once again that if the government had the will, we believe it could have eliminated $1,025 billion from its spending estimates. It could have taken about half of that money and given a tax break to the average Canadian, especially Canadians in the lower personal income tax brackets. The government could have given incentives to industry to allow it to get on with creating the jobs which are needed to lower our unemployment rate.
These are the hard facts, and I believe this government must recognize that, sitting at the top of the totem pole, it has access to funds to which no other governmental jurisdiction has access. We have pointed this out before. We have pointed out the fact that personal income tax is geared, under the present Income Tax Act, so that when the gross national product goes up, say 10 per cent, personal income tax goes up an arbitrary 15 per cent. There is no mystery about that. The fact is that personal income taxes at the federal level are bound to go up at a faster rate than the gross national product. The reason I emphasize that point is that this is why the government seems so inclined to spend money. The government is flush in revenue, and rather than do the honourable thing and give a tax cut, which in turn would create consumer demand, the government tends to cling to this revenue and work out spending programs which it feels it can get away with.
For those who were following the finance ministers' conference across the street yesterday, it was interesting to note the comments made by the minister of finance from Quebec, Mr. Jacques Parizeau. Dealing with this very question, he stated:
Only one tax can be said to have a natural increase rate significantly higher than the GNP increase rate, and that is the personal income tax. Come what may, every year this tax, even when indexed, produces some SI billion manoeuvring margin for the over-all Canadian governments. It represents nearly the total manoeuvring margin of governments in the long run-
Mr. Parizeau went on to state:
With the constitutional system being what it is, (no restriction on the federal power to expend funds, lack of precision on the respective jurisdictions at

December 7, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures
different levels of government) the use of this manoeuvring margin inevitably leads to excessive centralization of powers in Ottawa.
What Mr. Parizeau said has been stated many times, and surely it is time for this government to realize that by clinging on to this excessive revenue, which it has tended to do, and by spending that money, it is first of all creating the centralization to which Mr. Parizeau referred but, most importantly, it is acting as a drag on the economy. This government allows the federal treasury to be a drag on the economy to quite an extent, and that is why we have excessive unemployment at the present time. In short, we say the government should give a large proportion of that excess income tax revenue back to those who are paying the shot, the average wage earner, especially those earning $8,000 or less and certainly those earning less than $16,000 per year.
Through personal income tax, the average Canadian pays most of the tab for the extravagant spending habits of the present administration. In 1968, Canadians made up 34 per cent of total federal revenues through personal income taxes. By the end of this fiscal year federal income taxes levied on the average taxpayer will cover 53 per cent of federal revenue needs. In contrast, corporate income taxes contribute 15 per cent of revenues today, the same level as in 1968.
It is not the corporation, or even the wealthy individual, who bears the burden of federal spending; it is the worker, the little fellow, who has to cough up the money to finance the quadrupling of federal expenditures since 1968. In that connection, hon. members will recall that last night I pointed out that when this government took power in 1968, the total federal budget after 100 years of confederation was slightly under $10 billion. This year we have a budget of $42,250 billion, more than four times that of eight years ago when this government took power.
In my speech in this House on May 27, I indicated where more than $1 billion could be cut from federal spending and I reiterated those items last night. I suggest that one-quarter of this saving could be returned directly to the taxpayer, where it rightfully belongs. One-quarter could be used to get the economy moving again, and the remainder-about $500 million- could be applied to reduce the cash requirements of the federal government. This would give an indication that the present administration is trying to live within its means and there would be an opportunity for the private sector to borrow money at more reasonable interest rates.
Surely we should challenge the present administration to admit that its growth policies will never restore the losses in potential growth Canadians have suffered in the past two years. On this point, let us not forget that 760,000 Canadians continue to be jobless, and judging from the reactions during question period even today, that figure is not going to be broken by this government's actions in the foreseeable future. With a more imaginative approach at the federal level designed to encourage growth in our economy, the private sector could produce the jobs needed to get Canadians back to work. As the Economic Council of Canada pointed out, referring to possible changes in unemployment insurance regula-

tions which were announced by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen): "Regulatory changes alone do not, and will not, send people back to work if there are no jobs available."
During question period today I contrasted the experience in the United States with the experience in Canada, and perhaps for the record I should reiterate those rather startling figures. How often have those who wish to defend this government stood up and said that somehow the unemployment level in this country is better than that in the United States? Yet when we look at the figures we find that there are five provinces- Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland-which have higher unemployment levels than any state in the United States.
Half of our provinces are experiencing unemployment of approximately 10 per cent. That is the rate for Quebec, and in the case of Newfoundland, which has the worst rate, the rate is 14.8 per cent. The worst rate of any state in the United States is 9 per cent. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is confronted with these figures, he simply says that there is an international boundary between the two countries. Of course there is; that is the point we are making. Why is it that a country which is faced in many of its areas with similar problems to those in Canada has been more successful in bringing its state unemployment levels down compared with comparable provincial figures in this country?
Why should our five eastern provinces have consistently higher levels than, for example, any of the New England states? Why should the Atlantic provinces have an unemployment level of 11.8 per cent when the New England states have a level below 7 per cent? Surely it is time we started to ask these questions in this House. It is not enough to say that there is an international boundary between us. With the interrelationship there is between the Canadian economy and the American economy, we have to start finding out why the Americans have been more successful than we have in eliminating unfair distortions in unemployment levels on a regional basis.
One of the places we have to begin is by looking at the government's spending plans. If you were to ask businessmen for the most important reason the economy is not functioning better at the present time, you would be told it is because there is a deep lack of confidence in the business future of this country. If you were to ask why there is that deep lack of confidence, you would be told it is because of undue intervention at the governmental level, undue spending at the governmental level, and that in general there appears to be indecision at the government level about what the future holds for the economy in Canada. That is why the money is not being invested to create the jobs that would make us more competitive in world markets. There is lack of confidence. One of the key reasons for that lack of confidence is the high spending of this federal government which at the present time is outpacing the spending of all other levels of government.
December 7, 1976

As we know, there has been a great debate about what really causes inflation in a nation. Many people like to blame others-governments are blamed, business is blamed and labour is blamed. Surely one of the most fundamental reasons we have experienced the inflation we have in this country is excessive government spending.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that many people, in a rather apologetic way, now agree with that premise. They agree, for example, that the former minister of finance, Mr. Turner, was totally wrong in allowing federal spending to double in the 44 months he held that portfolio. I will say that, likewise, the public will generally feel that the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) would be wrong if he ever tolerated federal government spending to double again in 44 months since his taking over. That is the crunch; that is the problem on which we have to zero in. Let us not be thrown off the track by what the government represents as a restraint bill.
When we look at the key features of this bill, I think most of us will agree that much of it is window-dressing. For example, there is reference to disbanding the Company of Young Canadians. Mr. Speaker, that organization is dead and gone; people have not taken it seriously for several years. Can we really and honestly say that is is part of a governmental restraint program to disband it today? Information Canada has been criticized for many, many years. We believed it to be an improperly conceived and directed arm of government. To include it in a bill that is called a restraint bill is rather misleading.
A ceiling is, in effect, being put on family allowances in the sense that it will no longer carry the indexing into this year to allow it to equal last year's buying power. We have to ask the basic question: why was it right last year to give those who received the family allowance $20 in real buying power in terms of 1975 figures, but not give it in 1976 when the amount will be discounted by inflation? In buying power, in terms of 1975 figures, people may receive only $18.50 this year. Surely, before we pass this bill, we have to ask ourselves what the significant difference is between 1975 and 1976 to cause the government to say that, in terms of real buying power, family allowance cheques should be less this year than last year- especially when we look at the government's own spending program.
They suggest that government spending will be kept at last year's level. They, just arbitrarily, say they are going to restrain government spending to the rate of increase of the gross national product which, incidentally, includes 7 per cent or 8 per cent inflation. Arbitrarily they say, "Do not ask us to control our spending without allowing us to increase by the amount of inflation plus real growth in the economy." These are some of the questions that I hope hon. members will ask themselves before they bring debate on this bill to a conclusion.
Last evening I touched on the approach of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce to research and development in this country. There is a feature in the bill that is rather remarkable: before any new program is put in position,
Restraint of Government Expenditures before the government is able clearly to state what they intend to do to assist industry in this country to increase research and development expenditures, we find that if this bill is passed it will eliminate the present act governing research and development in industry. Why is that, Mr. Speaker? Surely, when we cite the unemployment figures, when we are faced with concrete evidence that one of the reasons for high unemployment is that our industry is losing its competitiveness in international markets, we must go to industry and offer incentives and inducements for it to undertake the research and development necessary to make it competitive in world markets. I would think that is elementary, yet this government does not appear to comprehend it.
The hard figures show that our industry is not as competitive as it should be. Is that any wonder, when we realize that in the past ten years the average amount spent per year on research and development by private industry in this country is .3 of 1 per cent? The United States, with its much greater gross national product, spends 1 per cent per year on research and development by private industry; for the last ten years Germany has spent 1.4 per cent, and Japan has spent 1.4 per cent. Rather than accepting the challenge to get up to the level with the United States, the government proposes, through this bill, to put an end to the only act we have that deals with the subject of research and development.
I am glad to see the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Faulkner) in the House today, Mr. Speaker. When his predecessor was confronted with this very serious situation he had the audacity to stand in this House and say that we did not realize when we were well off; that although Figures for research and development were lower in Canada, we should realize that we get the benefit of the research and development done by parent companies with branches here. What he was saying was that Canada should be glad to get second-hand merchandise; somehow research and development trickles into this country and we get the benefit after the parent company has had the advantage of breaking into world markets with new techniques.
That is the dilemma, Mr. Speaker. In the world's innovative market today, you cannot be a dealer in used merchandise and expect to be competitive with those who have the merchandise first: there is just no market for you; there is no room for you. If that is the case, why would the government be taking the retrograde step of cutting back on the unsatisfactory research and development commitment that this country has had for the last ten years?
For those reasons, among others, I believe hon. members have the right to debate this bill fully. They have tried to make the point that the government does not understand what restraint means. In short, we face another bill which is a bit of window-dressing. Say what you will, this government is a disgrace.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to participate in the debate on Bill C-19. After listening to the news and examining this bill, one is led to
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Ethier).]
wonder where the country is going. The Auditor General, in his report, gave us an inkling of what is happening in parliament. One sees a government opposite which will not heed the Auditor General's report. This government has possibly led the country into the worst mess we have seen in our time. Since the Auditor General recommended the appointment of an overseer of government spending, one cannot understand why the government should try to change his suggestion by setting up another royal commission. This government talks about restraint, Mr. Speaker, but it has got into a mess in pretty well all departments of government and is guilty of some of the most wasteful and corrupt expenditures we have heard of in our time.
In debating Bill C-19 one can talk of almost all departments of government. The Auditor General, after all, was appointed to report what he finds going on in the government. Since the government has failed to heed his recommendations, I think it only proper that we should deal with some of the matters he raised when we debate this bill. Consider how much money this government has wasted all through the years by setting up various royal commissions. Possibly the government set up its latest royal commission because it does not want the public to know all the truth just yet. Possibly in a couple of years, when present events will be behind us, it will reveal some of the things which have taken place.
I was thinking the other day of what the Liberal party had said about the Diefenbaker buck, or the "Diefen-dollar" as they called it, when the Conservative government some years ago devalued our dollar. I was wondering what they will say about the Trudeau buck. How will it look? Will the party opposite be ashamed of it?
According to news one hears, transportation in this country is in a mess. News stories I heard last night show that there is a transportation mess on the Pacific coast. We have heard maritime members speaking of what is happening in the maritimes, and westerners know what is happening in western Canada with regard to the user-pay concept of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang). Although I, personally, am not familiar with "at and east" rates, I know from listening to colleagues on my side of the difficult position in which the removal of these rates will place the maritime provinces and other parts of Canada. One is certainly forced to wonder what the effect will be in central and western Canada. We all heard last night what is happening on the Pacific coast and how that part of the country is reacting to the minister's user-pay concept. As well, recent revelations of the minister's own spending have not gone over well in the part of the country from which I come.
One hears much talk of rail operations. The minister has hesitated to state his position clearly on the Crow rates, for example. Western Canada would like to know where the minister stands on those rates. He must stop beating around the bush and tell us, because we very much want to know. One hears what has been happening at Mirabel and Pickering airports, and then one sees what is happening in central Canada and in the area I represent. I have attended, I do not know how many meetings to do with rail line abandonment. I
December 7, 1976

realize that the government has set up a commission to study the question, but it has no clear-cut policy.
Canadian National Railways advertises its rail passenger service. Mr. Speaker, in my area there is no rail passenger service-at least, there is no service at a convenient time. If there is such a passenger service, it is provided at the most outlandish hours when nobody can use it. Considering the high cost of energy and that rail lines have already been put down, I see no reason for not providing rail passenger service between places like Prince Albert, North Battleford and Edmonton. At present, no rail passenger service at all is provided to those areas. This makes one wonder if the government is serious when it says that it wishes to do something about passenger service.
Even on the freight haul service the trucks have pretty well taken over. One wonders why this has come about, because it is much more costly to build and maintain highways than to keep the present railbeds in proper shape. The way energy has increased in price, we should make more use of the railbeds. All across Canada the rail lines are becoming overgrown with grass and weeds. We hear a lot of talk about unemployment. I agree that there are some lines that could be abandoned. A lot of them should not have been put there in the first place. Railway companies were able to obtain charters which they should not have been able to get. A private railway company should not have been given a charter to build a line running parallel with another line. We all know the blunders that have been made. If we followed the user-pay concept, maybe all this would work out. Possibly we should do something about it. The Minister of Transport should come down to earth and give us an inkling as to where he is headed with his transport policy.

speechtext: I wish he would come down to earth.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Yes, he has been in the air too much- $740,000 worth. Western Canada is looking for a transportation policy from this minister which will straighten out the present mess. Year after year it is getting worse. There is talk of the CNR building rail lines in other countries. They should first look after Canada.
I want to deal briefly with agriculture. There is a big mess here, as well. The minister has brought forward a stabilization bill. Our party has always been in favour of a sound policy for the producer. Therefore, stabilization is very necessary. There are 30,000 permit-book holders under the Canadian Wheat Board who are not in the stabilization plan. They do not know where they are going. We also have Bill C-2, advance payments on farm stored grain. Many in this House will recall that the Diefenbaker government brought in a plan for farm-stored grain. It was put into effect overnight. The plan worked very well. The Liberals, who at that time were on this side of the chamber, said that it would not work and the members of the Wheat Board would quit. I never heard of any quitting. The plan carried on for years.
Restraint of Government Expenditures
We are certainly not opposing this new stabilization bill. However, when we see what it will cost the producers, we can see what the government is aiming at. Thousands more civil servants will be required to administer the plan. With the Diefenbaker plan, the farmer went to the elevator, swore an affidavit as to the amount of grain he had on hand, and went to the bank to get his cheque. It was a good plan and there was very little discrimination. We are hoping that this new plan will be workable. However, we cannot see the need for the extra cost that will be involved. The previous plan worked very well and there is no reason why it could not, again, be followed for payments on farm-stored grain.
Many farmers in my constituency are in a difficult situation. They were misled by this government to go into livestock. The farmers take a dollar less for their wheat, a dollar less for their barley, while everything is increasing in price-some of it by leaps and bounds. A few years ago the farmers were encouraged to go into livestock even though many of them were getting along very well growing grain. Today, many young people are being put out of business. Young farmers in my part of the country are discouraged. A few years ago, calves were selling as high as 72 cents a pound. The farmers borrowed money from the bank for cows that should have been canner cows. They were being paid $500 to $700 to raise calves because the government was saying, "go into beef'.
The government had better come forward soon with some kind of plan. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is in the chamber. For a year and a half he has been saying that he will come out with a plan, but the farmers are still waiting. The government must come forward with a plan to help not only western farmers but farmers in eastern Canada as well. I understand that they, too, are in a tough situation with regard to livestock.
My constituency extends as far north as the Northwest Territories. Therefore, I want to deal briefly with some of the problems being faced today by the people in the north. There are so many civil servants in the north, both federal and provincial, that they are tripping over each other. It appears as though the more people you have under you, the more important you are. The number of civil servants keeps increasing, but not the workload. There is a lot of unemployment in northern Canada, northern Saskatchewan in particular, that should not be. There should be some form of development which would put these people to work. The resources are there and the people are willing to work. Why not create employment, rather than have these people on welfare? I am sure they would much rather work.
Many people in my constituency are 25 and 30 years old and know no other way of life than welfare. If roads, railroads, and so on, were developed, many of these people could obtain employment. Instead, we sit here wasting time debating a bill that should never have come before the House at this time. We should have proceeded with the rest of our work in parliament. I am sure that this country is looking to parliament to get down to business and to do something about the mess into which the government has got the country.

Notwithstanding the fact that the reports of these commissions have not been fully completed and tabled, the government is proceeding on a piecemeal basis to dismantle the orderly shipment of grain in this country by attempting to remove, through clause 15 of the bill, section 272 of the Railway Act.

speechtext:
The parliamentary secretary, who is also aiding and abetting the minister, talks about a user-pay principle which will be applied uniformly across the country. The

fact of the matter is that this action of the government is a demonstration of the kind of user-pay policy we are going to see applied. The government is going to remove the statutory rates and revert to order in council assessment of subsidies for the movement of grain to replace the statutory provision. I presume that western grain farmers, millers and consumers will have to rely upon the whim of each and every government from now on under this new proposal, as opposed to having some concrete method of determining what the rates will be so that the industry can plan its future.
I hate to speculate, Mr. Speaker, but on the basis of my time in this parliament alone I think there is a plan on the part of the government to remove the statutory rates provisions, whether it be the "at and east" rates under the Railway Act or the Crowsnest pass rates. The actions of the government clearly indicate a move in that direction. For example, on Friday, November 26, the Minister of Transport announced a subsidy of $2.5 million to rapeseed processors to help them meet higher freight rates. Four days later, on Wednesday, December 1, the Canadian Transport Commission ordered the railways to increase freight rates for major domestic shipments of rapeseed oil, to reduce them for most export markets, and to raise both domestic and export prices for the transport of rapeseed meal. I understand that this particular move has been bitterly opposed by provincial governments, rapeseed producers and processors for some period of time during the course of this year.
If we look at this realistically, and if government members not on the treasury benches consider the direction in which the government is moving in regard to the shipment and movement of grain by rail, then I do not think there can be much doubt as to the intention of the government in regard to the Crowsnest pass rates. One of the first things that happened following my election to parliament was that the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board, the minister of transport, indicated in a speech in Edmonton that the government was going to give serious consideration to changing the whole present concept of the Crowsnest pass rates.

speechtext:
My colleague asks how he travelled to Edmonton. At that time I was not as cognizant as I am now of the method of travel of cabinet ministers. Under severe questioning by members of this side of the House, the minister indicated a basic and unequivocal interest in changing the whole concept and principle of the Crowsnest pass rates and in the statutory basis upon which they are founded.
Nothing that the minister has said since then leads me to believe the government has changed its attitude. Rather, all of the government's actions seem to point to a movement toward the so-called user-pay concept. As my hon. friend from Qu'Ap-pelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) pointed out-indeed, as members in this party from all parts of Canada did-we should be very leery indeed of the action taken by the minister regarding clause 15 of this bill. I think it is fair to say that if

the minister comes forward with a subsequent bill containing clause 15 of Bill C-19, I for one will not be in a position to support that kind of legislation, certainly not until I have had an unequivocal statement from the minister concerning his intentions regarding the statutory Crowsnest pass rates and I have found out exactly what is the policy of the government.
There has been no clear statement as to what the government has in mind. Rather, it resorts to the subterfuge of appointing a commission, of removing the protection of statutory rights, of giving a subsidy to a particular group of producers in western Canada. Surely, the intention is to raise the rates after the payment of a subsidy has been announced. What other conclusion could be drawn? They are attempting to do by the back door what they are afraid to do by the front door. If the government comes forward during an election with a proposition to remove the statutory protection of the Crowsnest pass rates, it does not know what trouble is in western Canada. I have spoken to many producers and farm groups about their attitude to this issue. The Minister of Transport and his colleagues had better be very careful before taking any action with respect to these rates which are the Magna Carta of the western grain farmer.
What makes a lot of people so mad about this bill that it was brought down following a statement by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in which he talked about a substantial reduction in the spending to which the government was committed. Since then we have had an opportunity of examining the legislation we have found, in the course of debate-the issue really concerns the report of the Auditor General-that the government in effect spills more in the course of a year than any bill of this kind could possibly save.
If the government is really interested in restricting its spending, it could do no better service to the taxpayer and to parliament than to give serious heed to the observations of the Auditor General. It should show more concern about its internal accounting processes. The only way in which there can be any substantial restriction in government spending is through a process of internal policing. It is true that it would be difficult, if not impossible, to reduce a lot of the expenditure which has to be made by statute. Nevertheless, there remains a vast area within which savings could be made if there were internal policing and effective scrutiny on the part of the Treasury Board. Equally to the point would be acceptance of the proposal made by the Auditor General with respect to a chief comptroller.
I was interested in the prepared question posed today by the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Martin) when he suggested to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) that it might be a good idea to put in place in each department some form of puisne chief financial officer. It seems to me that when the President of the Treasury Board goes to the trouble to write out a question to be asked by a member of this House, he and his colleagues must really be in a flap about the reaction in the country to their refusal to
Restraint of Government Expenditures accept a reasonable proposition on the part of the Auditor General.
What kind of argument do they really have to support their objection to this proposal? They say the official the Auditor General has in mind would somehow or other cause problems with respect to the working of our parliamentary system. If it was not pointed out by the Auditor General, it has certainly been pointed out by the members of the party to which I belong that these fears are groundless, that the proposal is quite consistent with our parliamentary system. The person to be appointed would not be an extra government official; he would fit right into the context of our present system, within the public service. However, knowing the limited capacity the government possesses, I compliment them at least on making some move toward self-policing.
I do not think any of us who have watched the administrative scene for any length of time has ever witnessed a government which has so demonstrated its lack of capacity to govern. It seems capable only of bungling and demonstrating arrogance toward those who are paying the bills. If they were really serious about restricting expenditure, they would not come forward with these television projects, the Prime Minister telling us all he intends to do to cut back spending, while at the same time sloughing off proposals for the effective policing of government expenditure by appointing a royal commission to look into the over-all question.
I do not think anyone is deluded as to the motives of the government in appointing this royal commission. The whole move is so transparent. The government wishes to remove this issue from the public forum and from discussion in parliament until after another election. One has almost to feel sorry for the members of the treasury benches when they feel the need to resort to this kind of subterfuge in order to get around a very serious situation, one which is recognized as such by every Canadian. If members would go back to their constituencies and ask their constituents what they felt was the most serious problem facing them with respect to the operation of government today, I believe most of them would say-

Possibly the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) would wish to elaborate on that statement. But in my opinion most people would say they are concerned chiefly about the lack of control over government spending. They see this in relation to their own businesses, to their own incomes. It is something they have seen personally, examples of which they bring to the attention of members of parliament presumably on both sides of the House.
I want to make brief reference to a part of the Auditor General's report which is receiving much attention now. I wonder if we will ever get to the bottom of it. However, I hope that the Standing Committee on Public Accounts will give its concentrated attention to the report. I am referring to the practice of the payment of commissions. I was interested to

December 7, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures read of the experience of the Americans with respect to the payment of commissions. For example, in the most recent edition of the Economist it was pointed out that there is a law in the United States which prohibits the payment of commissions in the distribution of food aid.
I think occasionally we can learn a lesson from our neighbours to the south. Very often we criticize them both for acts of commission and acts of omission, but I think they have been going through the difficulties of the Lockheed affair and problems that arise from that kind of transaction by a private company which is heavily funded by the government. They are also giving some attention to the question of the morality of paying commissions. I wonder whether this government is really serious about its position with respect to the efficacy of paying commissions in respect of foreign transactions.
I asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) last Friday whether any legal opinion had been given to the government by the Minister of Justice as the chief legal officer of the Crown regarding this whole issue. I was surprised to hear the minister say, in effect, that no such opinion had been given to the Prime Minister or to the cabinet. He simply sloughed off the question by saying that occasionally individual Crown corporations ask for legal opinions and are given them, but he did not address himself to the question of whether this cabinet had asked for a legal opinion as to whether their practice of paying commissions-particularly in the case of AECL, Polymer or Polysar-is in contravention of Canadian law. If there has not been an investigation of the legal consequences of these transactions, it shows that the government is not terribly interested in finding out what is going on.
I then asked the minister, in his capacity as acting solicitor general, whether there has been an investigation by any law enforcement agency of the activities of Canadian Crown corporations, and again the answer was an apparent undertaking by the minister to look into that matter and, I hope, to report to the House subsequently. However, the Minister of Justice is apparently prepared to turn aside the question by simply saying that the prosecution for any unlawful act is up to the provincial authorities. I wonder whether that is a good enough answer when we are talking about federal Crown corporations. We are not talking about individual citizens of one province or another, but about federal Crown corporations.
Is the Minister of Justice suggesting that somehow we in parliament should go to the provincial authorities and ask them to please investigate federal Crown corporations? The Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) has just come into the House, and I am glad to see him here. It seems to me that a rather unreasonable proposition was posed by the Minister of Justice last Friday in answer to my question.
What is the policy? Are we now to take the material about which the Auditor General has expressed his concern and address it to the attorneys general in the various provinces or, indeed, in any place where the federal government carries out its activities? Is there no responsibility on the part of the federal government to look into possibly unlawful or, indeed, illegal acts within its Crown corporations? I think these two

examples of answers to my questions show that the government is not at all anxious to get to the bottom of this matter- and one wonders why, without casting an innuendo or trying to suggest anything.
In its own interest, the government should attempt to get to the bottom of the matter, and if there have been wrongful acts I think the people of Canada will be far more appreciative of a government which comes forward with enthusiasm and vigour to investigate any possible wrongdoing than of a government that is merely prepared to sit back and let the public discover the facts through the medium of the press, from members of the opposition or from some public servant making a disclosure on the basis of an audit such as the Auditor General in his report.
I must say that the introduction of this legislation to the House could not have come at a worse time for the government. The government House leader will have to take a lot of trips to Paris to get away from this place and to contemplate what he can do to get the discussion about restraint of government spending off the floor of the House. It must be an agonizing experience for him to hear recounted over and over again, day by day, arguments and statements which prove without doubt that this government has lost its ability to control spending, has lost its capacity to govern and, indeed, has lost its will to govern our country.
I am glad to see that the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Goodale) is here, because I would like to repeat what he has said. I have to admit that he is here very often, and the people of Assiniboia must be very pleased that he is here so much of the time. But the fact of the matter is that I am very concerned about the statement made by the Minister of Transport, who is responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board, that clause 15 of Bill C-19 will be reintroduced, probably in this session of parliament. I can tell the minister, on the basis of what I have heard among my colleagues and in discussions across the floor, that at this point we have only warmed up to the big game. He will have a very interesting time if he tries to bring back the clause in another bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I want to point out that the attitude of some ministers, and primarily the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, is less than acceptable not only to hon. members on this side of the House but also to western Canadian grain producers. It has been adequately pointed out by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) that it is the intention of the minister to bring back clause 15 some time later in this session. We are not really talking about very much money when we relate it to the over-all budget of the federal government, but I suggest that the attitude of the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board is wrong.
Today I asked a question with regard to grain sales which have been made to speculators, and in his arrogant manner the minister tried to justify such sales. I do not think there is a Canadian today who knows exactly whether that sale was a good one or not, but the so-called high price the minister mentioned cannot be justified to the extent he would like to have it justified, primarily because those speculators do not have to pay for that grain for 12 months. That means that the Canadian producer has to carry the financing of those 160 million bushels of grain. On top of that, in one form or another, either on the farm or in storage facilities, the producer will have to store that grain. There is no agreement whereby the grain has to be delivered or paid for at the present time. Had there been one, I might have thought it was a good sale, but in view of the fact that this grain was sold to speculators there will be a new competitor on the world market with regard to grain.
It is generally agreed that there have been fairly good crops throughout the world this year, but there is no guarantee that
Restraint of Government Expenditures that will happen next year. The minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board should realize that unless there is an ample supply of moisture next spring there will be a drought on the prairies because there is no reserve whatsoever. If there is a recurrence of the dust-bowl of the 1930s, there certainly will be a market for that grain 12 months hence, and hon. members can imagine the profit the speculators will make on those 160 million bushels.
I would have no hesitation in selling that grain at the present time at present prices if it were going to people who needed it, or to consumers in other parts of the world who required it. I think the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board should take a second look at his attitude and his approach when he tries to justify sales of that nature.
I bring this to the attention of the House only because grain prices have dropped approximately $2 per bushel in a matter of 18 months, and it makes us wonder what is happening on the world market when the commissioner of the Canadian Wheat Board makes statements like he did last spring before the Standing Committee on Agriculture when he said that there were no forward sales to be made from May until September, and that the amount of barley which was being held by the Canadian Wheat Board was smaller than it had been for a long time. Canadian producers wonder what is actually happening when within months we go from a period of short supply to a time when there is such a drastic drop in prices and when the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board tries to defend policies of this nature. I realize that the minister is only human, but I think he should accept the fact that he might have made a mistake.
I am glad to see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) in the House this afternoon. I have a few words for him which have been voiced to me by many western Canadian beef producers. The minister has failed western beef producers in not having come forward during the past several weeks-and he should do so in the few days we have left before the end of the year-to tell the producers exactly what kind of economic climate will prevail for the marketing of their products in the months following the new year.
Everyone knows that the beef which will be coming to market in February, March, April, May and June of next year has to be going into the feed lot now. I believe the minister has really short-changed the producers by not telling them exactly what the import quota will be so that they could know whether to increase the amount of beef they put into the feed lot or whether they should cut back. This is a grave injustice, and the Minister of Agriculture is the one who is responsible, and who should be held responsible, for this situation.
The minister has come through some extraordinary periods of oversupply as well as periods of undersupply. If he is going to serve the industry as Minister of Agriculture, he should at least make an attempt to play ball with the producers. They can only know what the situation is if he tells them what the amount of imports will be after the new year. The minister has been jumping from crisis to crisis, and I presume that is what

December 7, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures
is going to happen after the new year. Probably we will not know what the quota is for the next year until then.
I was disappointed to learn that we are not to have a delegation at the discussions now taking place in the United States on the question of the over-all quota that is to be allowed into that country. I understand that Mexico will request that their quota be increased. If they succeed, I think it is fair to assume that our quota will be cut. It would certainly be in the interests of Canadian producers to have someone there.
Mr. Speaker, these are just a few short observations on matters that should be considered by the Minister of Agriculture and the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board. I respect the government for attempting to effect cut-backs in spending. It is a time for restraint, but a great deal of caution must be exercised if the government is not to become pennywise and pound foolish. Not only the well-being of producers could be jeopardized, but the whole economy could be hurt, because we rely to a considerable degree on agricultural production. I hope the minister will take my comments seriously and will rise in his place to tell Canadian beef producers what they may expect in the new year.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for affording me the opportunity to put these comments on the record.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the next few minutes, let me attempt to suggest to the government a few ways to save the taxpayers' dollars. However, I urge that it not be done at the expense of those who are eligible for family allowances or of the unemployed. Consequently, I shall use some Statistics Canada figures. The number of employees of that agency has reached 5,500 from 2,500 in 1967, which represents approximately a 120 per cent increase. The situation is quite the same in all other important departments.
Mr. Speaker, I was expressing in absolute figures and in percentages the increase in the number of public servants in only some of the most important departments because it would take too much time to give a comprehensive list. We should take note of the rates of increase since 1966. In 1975, there were 2,500 employees in the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, up 122 per cent from 1966. There are now 6,201 civil servants in the External Affairs Department, or 100 per cent more than in 1966. The Department of Energy, Mines and Resources has 8,646 civil servants, 99 per cent more than

in 1966. With 8,406 civil servants, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce has 81 per cent more staff.
To close that list, I shall add that in 1960 there was one civil servant in the federal Department of Agriculture for every 87 farmers. Mr. Speaker, it is quite ironical to see that, as the number of farmers decreased, that of the civil servants increased. Thus, in 1966, there was one civil servant for every 59 farmers whereas today, in 1976, there is one civil servant for approximately every 44 farmers. It all works quite well, doesn't it? The result we get are quite sufficient to prove that fact.
Mr. Speaker, it is quite interesting to note that if the number of civil servants increases, that of their travels by plane increases too, at a vertiginous speed, almost as fast as sound. Federal civil servants fly more an more, so much so that the cost of their travels has almost doubled over the last 30 months. According to the figures from Statistics Canada which I have here, federal civil servants flew 153,795 times in 1974-104,100 more flights than in 1973.
And during the first half of 1975, our dear traveling pen-pushers, namely our dear bureaucrats, took to the air at least 94,146 times. The cost of tickets also soared from $16.1 million in 1973 to $24.8 million in 1974 and over $16 million for the first semester of 1975 alone.
Mr. Speaker, we are without a doubt experiencing an "inflation" period of civil servants. By the way, it can easily be noted that the Parkinson law, according to which work expands to fill the time available for its completion has been applying to Canada ever since the Liberal party took office.
In 1954, British economist Colin Clark had this to say: "In any country a taxation rate of over 25 per cent seriously harms production and dangerously induces the consumer to spend more."
And he went on to say: "The price to pay will be inflation, taxpayers revolting and finally the destruction of the national economy and the democratic system."
We are realizing that today, for with an inflation rate of 11 per cent it is useless to ask ourselves whether Clark's theory was founded. As a matter of fact, if we look carefully at statistics, we see that civil service proliferation, which is in my opinion very disorderly, started to go out of sight in the 60's and government participation in the economy had reached 40 per cent in 1975. I say this, Mr. Speaker, to show that if a growing number of Canadians are employed by the government or draw most of their income from it, the risk is that the civil service might well become a state within the state, powerful enough to prevent the federal government from restraining its expenditures, as it wants to do. At the present time, the government of Canada employs over 1,200,000 Canadians, that is one out of eight workers, or 12 per cent of those on the labour market.
This costs the state in wages and salaries about $10 billion anually, that is about 15 per cent of our gross national
December 7, 1976

product. Governments, either municipal, provincial or federal, have become big employers, competing without difficulty with service industries, small businesses, the manufacturing industry, and so on.
There is another area, Mr. Speaker, where it would be quite possible in my opinion to save a great deal of money. The Progressive Conservative party is presently making much of various scandals and cases of bribery. This, of course, does not mean that I approve of scandals, but while I admit that there is cause for reflection and particularly that immediate action is required to do away with such scandals and bribery, it must be realized nevertheless that with the number of public servants I have just mentioned, it is very difficult for any government to control or at least have an absolute control over each individual. Still, in my opinion, there is a much more serious scandal, one which is draining several millions every hour of the day, every day, to the point that soon all the income and other taxes will only serve to pay the interests on the national debt and there will be no more money left for administration purposes. And yet, except for us, of the Social Credit Party of Canada, no other opposition party ever mentions it.
With your permission, Mr. Speaker, for hon members' benefit I would like to recall briefly certain truths about our economy and the national debt, an area where we stop the continuous devaluation of our dollar from which only financial sharks stand to benefit.
Mr. Speaker, a debt, whether private or national, is like a cancer eating away at the vital energy of our civilization, not only in Canada but elsewhere in the civilized world. The gross and net national debts have increased continuously in Canada since 1867. Indeed, if we consider the total debt of the federal administration, we find that in 1867, at the time of Confederation, the total national debt amounted to $93 million. In 1900, it had gone up to $346 million. In 1933, that is during the 50 year period following Confederation, it soared to $3 billion, and to $9,228 billion ten years later; it stood at $17,952 billion in 1955, and kept on rising until today when we are nationally indebted to the tune of $55 billion. I mention this, Mr. Speaker, to get to the point I was making a bit earlier on, that is to try to make the government understand that it should have restrained its expenses and if you will bear with me, I will try to show how it could have been done. There was therefore an annual average increase of 14 per cent.
In 1967, the national debt accounted for 33.9 per cent of the gross national product and 99.1 per cent in 1974. This marked increase indicates without a doubt the continuous tendency of governments to gobble up a greater part of a country's income. Finally, barely 100 years after Confederation, the Canadian national debt has been increased by about 60,000 per cent. Granted, the Canadian population has increased sixfold since Confederation but during that same period the government debt has been multiplied 600 times over. That is why every day Canadians pay $9 million in taxes, simply to cover the interest on this enormous debt.
Nine million dollars a day, how many bridges, hospitals, schools, public services which the Canadian population had to
Restraint of Government Expenditures do without does that represent? Nine million dollars a day going to financiers while the Canadian taxpayers keep on waiting for public services that are theirs by right and are paid for by their taxes. There is no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that the governments which allowed the public debt to increase without control are responsible for the shameless waste of $9 million a day in interest on the public debt. This money should be used instead to meet the needs of the citizens, not to enrich financiers.
As everybody knows, Mr. Speaker, some people generally distrust statistics but one must admit that it is sometimes good to be wary about the meaning of certain statistics; however I sincerely think that the figures I just gave reflect hard truths and realities. In particular, people realize that the system in which we live is really sick, and current events stand as proof of that. It can also be noted that debts incurred for public works never stop. Indeed, those debts will never be reimbursed because the present monetary system makes it almost impossible. Even if we succeed in reducing this debt, once again it is because the government takes the money from the taxpayers' pocket. And what if the government should fail to reduce it? Only this; taxpayers are called upon to bleed themselves white all their life, simply to pay for the interests.
As a matter of fact, it has been demonstrated that in Canada we are still paying for the interests on debts which were incurred in the past to produce goods which, in some cases, no longer exist. Furthermore, Treasury bills and bonds are the only instruments of the federal government's debt in Canada, and as these are issued to renew old loans rather than to refund them, the old debt and the interests keep growing.
Mr. Speaker, all hon. members and ministers know very well that each new loan starts the relentless process of compound interest. Each time a public debt is incurred, the public wealth of Canada is used as a guarantee to private credit monopolies. In other words, this means that our children become responsible for a growing national debt.
This also means that we will have to pay more taxes and to face a higher cost of living because in fact, this loan is nothing but a differed tax which will be shouldered sooner or later by the taxpayers. Every additional debt we make deprives us a little of our precious freedom which makes life worth living, since we are now enslaved to debts which hold us back and prevent us from speaking out as free individuals in a free society.
Mr. Speaker, indebtedness is sown by governments and taxes are the bitter crop harvested by the people, because as time goes on, one can readily realize that more and more the main function of any government is to levy taxes and to devise increasingly cunning methods of depriving people of their money. As for taxes, we have the personal income tax, the corporation income tax and the tax on dividends.
Mr. Speaker, it has already been evaluated that over 150 different taxes are levied on as simple a product as a loaf of bread. If we give ourselves the trouble of retracing them, we

December 7, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures
realize how many additional taxes are levied at each step in the production of a loaf of bread, at the various agricultural, processing and distribution levels. In addition, we all know that out of each dollar taken away from the people by the government in the form of taxes, 13 cents go immediately to the financiers to reimburse the interest of our debts.
I agree that under our present financial and monetary system, our governments must accept that the debt should increase continuously. That debt, as well as the high interest on it, must be reimbursed through taxes which are the very basis of inflation. But it must also be recognized that, at the same time, a chaotic and obsolete economic system is thus being perpetuated. At the present time, banks and other lending institutions lend money according to such principles as, for instance, that which demands that borrowers have guarantees, that the borrower be able to produce the goods and services promised, that the borrower be able to reimburse his loan; but, what if the borrower does not meet one or several of those requirements? What then? Just this: the borrower will not longer be able to borrow money.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that, as a nation, we meet all the requirements, as we own tremendous guarantees such as our lands, our forests and our natural resources. In addition, we are in a position to produce all the goods and services we need.
I think it would be normal to replace the financing of the national debt by issuing federal funds: this way, perhaps the money supply will not increase, but at least we will not have any useless interest to pay. Let us suppose for instance that a community decides to build a school at a cost of about $1 million. It is now proven that a community, which has an excellent reputation or enjoys a high credit rating, can borrow money on national and international markets at an agreed interest rate. In addition, most of the time financing is done through bonds guaranteed by municipalities or through other financial sources.
So the community is now said to have contracted a debt. Thus a school is built to the advantage of the residents and to do so we used our own material and labour. However, to reach our end we have to borrow $1 million to be paid for instance at 10 per cent over 25 years-a total amount of $2,683,500. One thing for sure anyway, the money will be found to pay that debt. But it is really interesting to see how it is going to be done. I think that once again we are going to get this money through higher taxes.
But we must bear in mind, Mr. Speaker, that if our country could issue that money through the Bank of Canada, we would have to repay only the initial amount, $1 million in this case. Then the $1,683,500 in saved interest could be transferred to the community through tax reductions. Moreover, by reducing the direct cost the community has to pay for this school through elimination of interest payments, we would fight inflation.
Anyway, I think that if the federal government can afford to put hundreds of millions of dollars at the disposal of other countries for 15, 20 and even 50 years, always without any interest, it should certainly be able to lend money to provincial

and local administrations at interest rates not exceeding the administration charges, and the best way the government could put this into practice overnight would be to grant these loans to municipalities which need them.
All this, Mr. Speaker, for it is already five o'clock, to state clearly that if our government wants to save money, restrain its operating expenditures and ensure sound and effective management of taxpayers' money, it has to make sure that the national debt does not increase and stop borrowing money at interest rates of 10 and 12 per cent. I think that would be one way of giving Canada a flourishing economy and sound financial management.

Order, please. There seems to be a disposition to agree with the suggestion that has been made, but before asking consent I want things to be clear. We would need consent to suspend the debate. that Bill C-9, to approve, give effect to and declare valid certain agreements between the Grand Council of the Crees (of Quebec), the Northern Quebec Inuit Association, the Government of Quebec, la Societe d'finergie de la Baie James, la Societe de developpement de la Baie James, la Commission hydro-electrique de Quebec and the Government of Canada and certain other related agreements to which the Government of Canada is a party, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by thanking all hon. members for agreeing to suspend the private members' hour for this important debate. I apologize to the hon. member for

Selkirk (Mr. Whiteway). I thought that someone was speaking to him about the suspension of the private members' hour, but it seems I was mistaken.
Mr. Speaker, in the Speech from the Throne the House was advised that the government intended to introduce legislation respecting the James Bay and northern Quebec agreement. I am pleased, as Minister of Indian Affairs, to move second reading of Bill C-9, an act to approve, give effect to and declare valid the James Bay and Northern Quebec agreement, which is an important landmark in relations between our native peoples and the Canadian government.
The James Bay and Northern Quebec agreement demonstrates very clearly the federal government's recognition of its obligations toward the Indians and Inuit of that territory. As a comprehensive claims settlement, the agreement acknowledges the traditional use and occupancy of the land by the Indians and Inuit of northern Quebec. The legislation which I recommend to this House merits the support of all members because it will enable the native peoples of James Bay and northern Quebec to determine their own future, political, economic and social evolution.
In recommending this legislation to parliament the government is fulfilling an obligation it assumed in signing the agreement to introduce legislation implementing the terms of the agreement. As a co-signatory to the agreement, the province of Quebec has assumed a similar obligation and, accordingly, the national assembly adopted the corresponding provincial legislation on June 30, 1976. It is anticipated that upon adoption by parliament the federal and provincial enactments will come into force simultaneously through respective proclamation by the governor in council and by the lieutenant-governor in council.
On this occasion I should like to acknowledge the important contributions of the many individuals who made the negotiated settlement possible, members of the Cree and Inuit associations, many of whom are here for this historic debate, officials from the Quebec government and its agencies, and from the federal government. In the context of the history of the agreement, I want in particular to pay tribute to the efforts of chief Billy Diamond of the Cree, and Mr. Charlie Watt of the Northern Quebec Indian Association, both of whom are here today-
