speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: JAMES BAY AND NORTHERN QUEBEC NATIVE CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO GIVE EFFECT TO AGREEMENTS WITH NATIVES OF NORTHERN QUEBEC
speechtext:
-as well as to my predecessors in this office, the present Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) and the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Buchanan). Bill C-9 results from the dedication of all the parties and of their determination to arrive at a negotiated settlement.
The area covered by the proposed legislation comprises 410,000 square miles, or about 60 per cent of the province of Quebec and, incidentally, almost the size of the entire province of Ontario. It has a population of about 20,000 people, including some 6,000 Crees and 4,000 Inuit, and is rich in wildlife, forest and mineral resources. The background of the agree-
December 7, 1976

ment to which the legislation will give effect is complex. I shall outline some points which I believe will be useful in affording a better understanding of the bill. In 1898, Quebec's northern boundary was extended by statute to the Eastmain River without any reference to Indian rights. In 1912, the Quebec boundaries extension act transferred the area north of the Eastmain River from the Northwest Territories to the jurisdiction of Quebec. It also assigned an obligation to the provincial government to settle land claims which native people in that area might raise, in much the same manner as the government of Canada had dealt with the rights of Indian people in other parts of the country.
However, the obligations under the Quebec Boundaries Act were not pursued until 1971, when the provincial Dorion commission recommended that the province reach an agreement to recognize the rights of native people in that territory. In the same year, the province of Quebec announced its intention to develop the hydroelectric power resources of the James Bay territory and subsequently established the James Bay Development Corporation. This announcement, coupled with expressions of concern about their land rights from the Crees, who were most directly affected, led to periodic meetings between officials of the Department of Indian Affairs, Cree representatives and, in turn, the provincial officials concerned. A tripartite committee considered the whole range of questions raised by the native peoples of the James Bay area.
In October, 1971, the federal government provided funds to the Indians of Quebec Association to enable it to inform native people in the area about the proposed development. During the next two years the main effort was directed toward persuading the provincial government to address itself more directly to the concerns expressed by the native population. In the meantime, my predecessors gave both moral and financial support to the Indians. By the end of 1973, $981,000 had been provided to enable them to pursue their claims and to conduct intensive research into the effects of the development scheme.
It must be remembered that the federal government has also been involved in environmental matters in the James Bay area since 1971. In July of that year an environmental study group, composed of provincial and federal representatives, was formed to study the ecological impact of the proposals. The preliminary report, released in February, 1972, stated clearly that the impact of the proposed development on the native population of the area was the most pressing question to be resolved. Acting upon its recommendation, an agreement was signed between Environment Canada and the James Bay Development Corporation for the purpose of gathering sufficient data to have an adequate knowledge of the ecosystem. This is considered an essential prerequisite for conducting an eventual impact assessment of the project. This agreement now has been extended until March, 1979.
When discussions over the next two years failed to yield satisfactory results, the Indians and Inuit sought an interim injunction to halt the James Bay project. The federal govern-
James Bay Agreement
ment provided financial assistance to the Crees and Inuit in pressing their claims in the courts. In November of 1973, Mr. Justice Malouf of the Quebec Superior Court ruled in favour of the native peoples. Shortly thereafter, the Quebec Court of Appeal reversed that decision, thereby allowing the continuation of the project. It has been suggested on several occasions that the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development should have been more involved in this action, and even that the department itself should have taken the case to court. On the contrary, the Indians and Inuit themselves wished to take the leading role, and they had every right to do so. They told the federal government that they wanted to take the lead if we would provide support. In fact, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development provided a total of approximately $5.5 million in the form of grants and loans in support of their research and other court and negotiating costs.
In January of 1974, the Quebec government announced an offer of settlement which was deemed satisfactory by the parties concerned as a basis for negotiation. In order to ensure that the position of the Indian and Inuit groups was safeguarded and supported, federal authorities became formally associated with the negotiations. An agreement in principle was reached in November, 1974, and a year later the final agreement was signed after detailed negotiations involving representatives of the federal government, the Crees, the Inuit, and the province of Quebec. During the course of the negotiations, continuous information and consultation, with financial support by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, took place within the native communities. It was established, however, that a confirmation process would be carried out in accordance with clear guidelines set down by the department.
I should add that the northern Quebec Inuit Association and the General Council of Cree of Quebec took the initiative to explain the agreement in separate meetings held in the 22 native communities. Summaries of the agreement in Cree and in Inuit were prepared and used by the two associations for this purpose. The vote in the Indian and Inuit communities gave overwhelming support to the final agreement, more than 95 per cent of those who voted, and 66.5 per cent of the eligible Inuit voters actually voted. Of those, 1,253 voted in favour of the agreement, and 45 against. While only 25 per cent of the Cree eligible voters participated in the confirmation process, they supported the agreement 922 to 1. The small percentage of Cree voters, however, can be explained by the extensive consultation which the Cree themselves carried out up to the signing of the agreement.
As hon. members are probably aware, there was some opposition to the James Bay agreement by potential beneficiaries. Sizeable groups in three Inuit communities-Povung-nituk, Sugluk and Ivujivik-criticized, in particular, the concepts of extinguishment of rights, the categorization of lands and regional government. Last August federal officials, along with the Quebec minister of natural resources, met with representatives of these communities to discuss their concerns. The meeting served to clarify the interests and the provisions
1754

James Bay Agreement
of the agreement in respect of the main concerns of the three communities.
At that time the Inuit were told that the agreement had been nogotiated in good faith by all the parties involved. It was also indicated that the governments would be prepared to consider and discuss with the other signatories to the agreement any proposals worked out with, and put forward by, the NQIA to change the implementation phase to better meet the requirements of the communities, but it was made clear that the main principles of the agreement could not be changed.
While I am sensitive to their concerns, I am confident that if these groups were to sit down with the rest of the Inuit community in that territory in order to deal with their differences, workable solutions could be found which would benefit all the Inuit of northern Quebec. Billy Diamond, chief of the Grand Council of the Crees of Quebec, gave his assessment of the James Bay agreement before the Berger inquiry last June. He said:
The James Bay Crees have put themselves in an autonomous and independent position, not only to face the government of Canada and of Quebec, but also to face the society which they will have to participate in, not as spectators, but as p*articipators and decision-makers of their future.
The majority of native people who approved the negotiated settlement did so because they agree that it will enable them to participate as decision-makers of their future and that it will provide them with the resources necessary to effectively meet their needs while, at the same time, preserving their traditional cultures.
The legislation now before the House is fully consistent with the federal government's established policy. More than three years ago, in August 1973, the minister of the day clearly acknowledged the government of Canada's willingness to negotiate with Indian and Inuit representatives as follows:
Claims related to the loss of traditional use and occupancy of lands in certain parts of Canada where Indian title was never extinguished by treaty or superseded by law.
These claims are known as comprehensive claims. The policy recognized that such claims were not only for money or land but involved the possible loss of a way of life, or at least major adjustements, for which native peoples must be compensated through cultural, social and economic benefits established by mutual agreement. While committing the federal government to a key role in any claims negotiations, it was emphasized that settlements could be satisfactorily reached only if the province or territory concerned participated along with the federal government in the negotiation, settlement and compensation process.
The new land regime created by the agreement which this legislation will make effective is a major component of the specific rights and benefits conferred on the Cree and Inuit residing in the James Bay and northern Quebec area. It will support, in a significant manner, the native economy of the territory which has been traditionally based on hunting, fishing and trapping. It will enable the native peoples in that area to continue to derive their livelihood from these activities if they choose to do so.

In general terms, the land regime encompasses the James Bay Cree population south of the fifty-fifth parallel and the Inuit communities north of that latitude. Lands in the territory have been divided into three broad categories: the first is the areas around the Cree and Inuit communities; the second is generally the adjacent land which they have traditionally used for hunting, fishing and trapping; and the rest comes under the third category definition.
Category 1 lands, consisting of the areas in and around the 22 Cree and Inuit communities, are reserved for the sole use and enjoyment of the native people and will be largely self-administered by local and regional councils. On these lands the Crees and Inuit will have exclusive hunting, fishing and trapping rights. They will also enjoy exclusive rights to the forests and soapstone deposits for both personal and commercial use.
While mineral and subsurface rights will belong to Quebec, any development must be approved by the native communities involved. The provincial government will also be permitted limited expropriation rights for necessary public services such as roads and transmission lines, but any lands so used must be replaced or compensated if such works interfere with native activities.
With respect to the Crees, the category 1 lands will be divided into 1A lands, under federal jurisdiction, and IB lands, under provincial jurisdiction. The 1A lands, which will include the existing communities, in most cases will in some ways resemble Indian reserves elsewhere in Canada. Ownership of the IB lands will be vested in provincial corporations controlled by the native people. These corporations may not, however, sell or cede the land to anyone but the province of Quebec.
The second component of the land regime, category 2 lands, are those where the Crees and Inuit will again have exclusive hunting, fishing and trapping rights but no special right of occupancy. The Quebec government may develop these lands, but the native people must be granted replacement lands or compensation. Mining will be permitted as long as it does not unreasonably hamper native harvesting of the land.
In the remainder of the territory, category 3 lands, the native people will be entitled to hunt, fish and trap year round, and certain species will be reserved for their exclusive use. They will also have forest and outfitting privileges.
Land is intrinsic to the way of life of native peoples and is only one of the benefits provided by the agreement. The detailed and lengthy agreement provides them with other resources to improve and strengthen their position and role in contemporary society while enabling them to maintain their traditional cultures. Provisions aimed at giving the Crees and Inuit of James Bay and northern Quebec the opportunity to manage or participate effectively in the management of activities which affect their interests are major features of the agreement.
The Crees and Inuit will have an equal voice on the coordinating committee which will deal with all questions and
December 7, 1976

problems relating to the hunting, fishing and trapping regime. This committee can, for example, make recommendations to the appropriate level of government to regulate harvesting activities; it can set quotas on the harvesting of certain wildlife species.
To ensure further that the Crees can maintain their traditional way of life by harvesting wildlife, provincial legislation has been adopted providing for an income security program. At the same time a support program which will be managed by the Inuit will guarantee supplies of hunting, fishing and trapping produce to those unable to harvest for themselves and will facilitate exchanges of produce among communities.
The Indians and Inuit will also participate in policing the hunting, fishing and trapping regime, and both the federal and provincial governments have undertaken to provide the necessary training. Above the 55th parallel a regional police force will be set up, with special training provided for the Inuit officers. South of the 55th parallel special Cree units of the Quebec Provincial Police are to be established as quickly as possible. Finally, the entire territory will be constituted as a single judicial district which will be served by itinerant courts to bring the administration of justice closer to the people the judicial system serves.
The agreement recognizes the continuing need for environmental protection to ensure that the land and wildlife are safeguarded for the native peoples from the effects of industrial and commercial activities. The Crees will have equal representation with the James Bay Energy Corporation in determining remedial works needed to minimize the effects of hydro-electric undertakings south of the 55th parallel.
An agency to be called La Grande Complex Remedial Works Corporation will provide $30 million for these works over 11 years. Furthermore, the Cree and Inuit people of the territory will have an equal voice with government officials in the administration and supervision of the environmental and social impacts assessment process regarding proposed industrial initiatives throughout the territory. The initiatives include mining, major forestry developments, and power plants.
For those Indian and Inuit people who choose to take part in the economic development of the territory, the opportunities will be there. Government assistance will be offered to groups or individuals to establish or expand business enterprises. Training and employment programs will help native people to obtain jobs in development activities or in government services. These measures and others to open up greater economic opportunities for the Cree people of the territory will be promoted by the James Bay Native Development Corporation.
The federal government and the province of Quebec will continue to provide programs, funding and technical assistance to the Inuit of the area, with greater emphasis on the promotion of economic viability and development in their communities. Government funding and technical assistance will be available for key local services such as community centres and sanitation. In addition, a joint economic and community development committee with a majority native membership will review and make recommendations concerning the various
James Bay Agreement
programs related to the social and economic development of the Indian and Inuit people.
The Cree communities will be independent of the municipality of James Bay, the organ of local administration for the rest of the territory south of the 55th parallel. North of the 55th parallel each Inuit municipality will be represented by one councillor in the Kativik regional government, which will have jurisdiction over municipal affairs. Throughout all the territory governed by the agreement the native languages, as well as English and French, will be languages of administration.
I should mention that a separate piece of federal legislation will be introduced at a later date to deal with local government and land administration on lands designated as category 1A. These lands, to be set apart for the exclusive use and benefit of the James Bay Cree bands, will be transferred to Canada's jurisdiction by Quebec. A new legislative framework is necessary since some of the benefits granted to the Crees under the James Bay and northern Quebec agreement are not provided for in the present Indian Act.
Under the provincial education act the Cree and Kativik school boards will respectively have jurisdiction over and responsibility for the elementary, secondary and adult education of the Crees and Inuit in the territory. These boards will have the powers and functions of education boards elsewhere in the province. The Cree and Kativik boards may also make agreements with Canada for additional educational programs not provided by the province and will provide education in the students' native language.
In regard to health and social services, the general laws of the province will apply. However, native management and administration of these services are ensured by the agreement through the establishment of a Cree regional board of health and social services and, north of the 55th parallel, of a Kativik health and social services council.
The foregoing are the main elements of the James Bay agreement. I would like to note two other factors which are directly related to native interests in the territory. A group of 400 Indians, the Naskapis of Schefferville, live in the area governed by Bill C-9, but they have not signed the agreement. Nevertheless, they have been negotiating with federal and provincial officials over the past year to obtain benefits and rights similar to those gained by the Crees and Inuit. Although general agreement has been reached on the most substantive issues, discussions are continuing on the few remaining aspects of the agreement.
As hon. members are all aware, I agreed to delay this bill momentarily to enable the Naskapis to reach an agreement because their interests in the territory are affected by the enactment of the legislation before this House. I met personally with their representatives in November to discuss these questions and I undertook at that time to give the Naskapis one month's notice before bringing Bill C-9 forward for third reading if they had not at that time reached an agreement in the negotiations with Canada and Quebec on their claim. Efforts are continuing to reach an agreement with them. In addition it should be noted that the Quebec government has
80005-43i/2

December 7, 1976
James Bay Agreement
undertaken to negotiate claims with any other native groups who may be able to establish an interest in the territory.
Negotiations are also under way between the federal government and the Crees and the Inuit regarding their traditional rights of use and occupancy on the offshore islands. These Northwest Territories islands are, in the main, situated within 15 miles of the Quebec shoreline in James Bay, Hudson Bay and Hudson Strait. During the course of the James Bay negotiations it was agreed that separate settlements would be concluded for these islands. We anticipate that agreement in principle will provide for special rights and regimes for the Crees and Inuit similar to those they obtained on the mainland. However, the Inuit of Port Burwell on Killinek Island in the Northwest Territories have been included in the James Bay agreement at their own request.
The Northern Quebec Inuit Association has made representations to both governments for amendments to certain sections of the agreement and to Bill C-9. I have met personally on two occasions with the Inuit representatives, in November and again earlier today. Discussions on these matters will continue between the Inuit, the federal government and, as required, hopefully with the province of Quebec. I have promised Charlie Watt, president of the Inuit of northern Quebec, that I will seriously and openly examine these amendments with the hope that an agreement can be reached on them prior to committee stage of this bill.
Among the issues the Inuit have raised is a request that Bill C-9 be amended to delete the provisions relating to the extinguishment of the native interests of the Inuit of Port Burwell across Canada pending an agreement on the offshore islands. At this point I believe that the best course of action is to pursue the negotiations with a view to reaching an early agreement. I have urged the Northern Quebec Inuit Association to join us at the negotiating table as soon as possible in an attempt to resolve this issue. If it becomes obvious that substantial progress cannot be made before the closing of the parliamentary committee discussions-and I hope progress will be made-I have assured the Inuit representatives that I am prepared to review the matter with them again before bringing Bill C-9 forward for third reading.
As you know, the Inuit have publicly raised certain issues with respect to the completion of their selection of lands. In this regard there have been meetings between the NQIA representatives and the province of Quebec, with the participation of a federal observer. I hope that these discussions will proceed favourably toward the resolution of the land selection issues, and that through the continued efforts of all parties a satisfactory agreement will be reached in the near future.
I am convinced all hon. members will agree that, in many ways, the Indian and Inuit people have been in a seriously disadvantaged position within our society. For this, we and our forefathers all share some blame. Although there have been some improvements in recent years, we must continue to rectify the imbalance. Participation in the vital decision-mak-

ing processes to which I referred will be facilitated by the financial compensation included in the agreement.
This compensation, totalling $225 million over 20 years, will be paid to and administered by Cree and Inuit controlled corporations for the benefit of all native people in the James Bay and northern Quebec territory. The federal government is committed to a cash payment of $32.75 million and the provincial government is to pay $42.25 million. An additional $75 million, guaranteed by the Quebec government, will be paid as hydro-electric royalties by the James Bay Energy Corporation. A final $75 million in Quebec government debentures will be provided to the native people in lieu of the original Quebec proposal for royalties from mining development in the territory. The agreement further provides for the exemption from taxation of the monetary compensation.
Because no land claims settlement can possibly solve all the problems of the native people concerned, such settlement must be accompanied by programs which increase economic opportunities and which encourage the native communities to develop their own institutions through education and training. The federal government is committed to the continuation of these programs which are included in the James Bay and northern Quebec agreement. All parties in the negotiations are convinced that such programs are necessary to enable the native people in the territory to participate fully in the economic, social and political structures of Canadian society, in their own way, while preserving the values which they cherish.
During recent months there have been criticisms of the use of the term "extinguishment of native rights" in the bill presently before the House. I would like to mention here that this term is not a new concept and was used in the prairie treaties, in the Alaska native land claim settlement, and in the James Bay agreement itself. In signing the agreement, the James Bay Crees and the Inuit of Quebec agreed to surrender their traditional interest in these lands in return for the specified benefits granted to them under the agreement and at the same time agreed to the term "extinguishment". If hon. members or others who come before the parliamentary committee have a better way of expressing this concept, I for one would be willing to consider their suggestions. The government's policy is based on the concept that the settlements reached must be final, foreclosing the possibility of future claims, based on historical use and occupancy of the lands concerned, by the native parties to such settlements.
It should be eminently clear that the agreement and the legislation which the House is asked to endorse confer specific rights and benefits on the Cree and Inuit people of the James Bay and northern Quebec territory. Previous to the agreement and Bill C-9, the native people of that territory had traditional, unspecified rights which have never been clarified in Canadian law. Until now these rights had not been sanctioned or protected by treaties or laws in that territory. Such uncertainty and vagueness will disappear upon giving legal status, acceptable in our courts of law, to well-defined rights and benefits through the proposed legislation. In addition to the specific rights and benefits outlined in the agreement, Bill C-9 ensures the Cree

and Inuit people in the territory that they will continue to enjoy all the rights and benefits to which all Canadian citizens are entitled, as well as those resulting from the Indian Act and any other eventual legislation applicable to them.
Other claims negotiations are currently taking place for the Yukon, the Northwest Territories, and British Columbia. The federal government is committed to a flexible approach, recognizing that different native groups in various areas of the country have different needs and priorities, as well as distinct characteristics. Bill C-9 and the agreement which it approves contain components such as hunting, fishing and trapping rights, environmental guarantees and increased local autonomy, which for the sake of fundamental equity could well apply to other settlements. However, our approach recognizes that unique problems and conditions require different arrangements, and therefore, agreements which are best suited to the people and areas concerned.
It is my sincere belief that this flexible, dynamic approach in the ongoing consultations and negotiations with the Indian and Inuit people will provide a sound basis for the just settlement of their land claims and will ultimately serve to safeguard their identity within Canadian society.
I would urge hon. members to give quick passage to this bill at second reading so that it can be sent to committee for the appropriate hearings where all concerned can present their views. I believe that such hearings by the committee will clear up any misgivings and misunderstandings that hon. members might have. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I thank all hon. members for their attention in this important and historic debate.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to compliment my colleague, the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Whiteway), for relinquishing his time between the hours of five and six this afternoon in order that we could initiate this

December 7, 1976
James Bay Agreement
most important debate on Bill C-9. Of course he did this so that members from the Cree and Inuit community could listen to the initial portion of the debate in the House of Commons.
I understand there has been some agreement to permit the hon. member for Selkirk to proceed with his private member's bill perhaps some time next week. I am certain that all members of the House will support that piece of legislation which is extremely important and vital. In relinquishing his time, the hon. member made a major concession of that portion of our parliamentary system which is scrupulously guarded by all members of parliament. I believe, however, this will not establish a precedent that will be followed in the House. I am equally certain that those individuals referred to previously, the Cree and Inuit who travelled so far to listen to a portion of the debate, will appreciate and commend the hon. member for his gesture in relinquishing that time this afternoon.
I listened with great interest to the comments of the minister this afternoon. Without appearing to be too critical, I felt for the most part of his speech that I was in effect reliving one of my mundane history courses from earlier years. However, toward the latter part of his speech the minister referred specifically to his involvement with the Naskapis, the problems of offshore islands, and the Inuit at Port Burwell. I sensed that the minister was inferring there would be a new purpose, a new sense of direction or new morality in the department with his arrival to that portfolio. May I simply say we would appreciate and welcome that type of action. Indeed my party would support that type of initiative from the minister. However, I must remind the minister that, by virtue of his presence in the cabinet prior to his recent appointment, he was obviously privileged and briefed on the issues and decisions that were taken by the Liberal government in the handling of the James Bay issue.
I have confidence in the minister's integrity. In saying that, I am sure he will not attempt to impart to this House or the committee an aura of innocence regarding the facts leading up to the James Bay agreement and the introduction of this legislation. If by chance our historical facts should not jive or if they should be at odds, I am certain the minister will be prepared to defend the government's position when this bill is referred to committee.
The problems of native people are written in the statistics of short-life expectancy, increased infant mortality, mercury poisoning, unemployment, poor housing, and poverty. There is a need for a firm commitment on the part of government to rectify these problems, and the land settlement provides Canada with a unique opportunity to take an important step in that direction.
This bill which enshrines the James Bay agreement and the northern Quebec agreement in legislation has numerous parameters, many of which the minister referred to in his speech this afternoon. I have no doubt that many of these will be examined during this debate and during subsequent standing committee hearings. However, it is important that all

members understand the basic issue in this debate, that of a minority group and its future.
We are talking about individuals, whether they be grandparents, parents, children, isolated Inuit hunters in the Arctic Circle, Cree trappers from the interior, or the forgotten Naskapis who bear earlier scars from encounters with government. These Indians and Inuit are simply asking that we listen and understand. They are simply asking for the opportunity to grow, to develop and contribute to our Canadian society. They are asking for nothing more than to be recognized in their own right as the original inhabitants of the James Bay area. In failing to recognize this basic issue, the government has violated a principle fundamental to our democratic society, a principle which has sustained the growth and development of Canada through the interdependence of numerous minority groups.
I want to indicate that I sincerely hope the final settlement will fulfill the aspirations of the native signators to the agreement. However, it is my personal belief, after a thorough analysis of the circumstances surrounding the settlement, that the signing of the agreement on Remembrance Day, November 11, 1975, is prophetic, and future historians will record it was the native people who made the sacrifices; not the power hungry corporations insensitive to the needs and aspirations of the native people; not the province of Quebec which for more than half a century ignored its obligations clearly defined in the Quebec Boundaries Extension Act of 1912, a province which was finally driven to the negotiation table only after the Indian chiefs of the project area began a suit against the James Bay Corporation, seeking an injunction to half the project; and not the Government of Canada, which from the outset abrogated its constitutional and trust responsibilities on behalf of native people.
It is impossible to separate the legislation and the agreement from the manner in which the James Bay project was initiated, an agreement which I must emphasize was signed by this government with full knowledge of all the facts, including the scandalous omission of native people from the final agreement on November 11, 1975. As Boyce Richardson stated in his book "James Bay":
Probably no other project of similar scale has ever been put on foot for such nakedly political purposes, and with so little attempt to disguise those political purposes.
The former premier of the province of Quebec in announcing the James Bay project in 1971, in order to fulfil an earlier election promise to provide 100,000 new jobs, made the decision without thought of the implications. He ignored earlier studies rejecting the project. He made the announcement of the now estimated $16 billion project before its economic viability was established. He rejected the necessity to determine the environmental consequences of such large scale intervention in the north and, more important, he did not acknowledge that the land in question was occupied and used by native people.
December 7, 1976

But, more important, I ask you, Mr. Speaker, what was the position of this federal Liberal government during that period when the isolated native communities, lacking political and economic power, faced extinction of their culture and life style, indeed their very lives, in a fight against powerful national and international interests behind the project? This federal Liberal government chose silence rather than speak of its constitutional responsibilities, and it chose inaction rather than fulfil its special trust responsibilities toward native people.
What should we have expected from this government? What role should this government have played in the James Bay litigation? Should not the government have been involved because of its constitutional and trust responsibilities? It is not my intention to review all relevant data. However, it can be stated that the policy of previous governments, for the major part of our life as a nation, has been recognition of native land rights. The one exception followed the introduction of the government's White paper on Indian policy in 1969 when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in responding to the question of the existence of aboriginal rights, stated:
Our answer, it may not be the right one and may not be the one which is accepted ... Our answer is, no.
But that declaratory policy was forced to change following the Nishga judgment by the Supreme Court in 1973. Then six judges agreed that aboriginal title exists, and the Prime Minister was compelled to state:
Perhaps you have more legal rights than we thought you had when we did the white paper.
May I add that the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) during the debate on April 11, 1973, clearly defined the position of the Progressive Conservative party, and our recognition of aboriginal rights.
In 1972 when the Indian chiefs from the James Bay area began a suit against the James Bay corporation seeking an injunction to halt the project, this federal government described its position as one of "alert neutrality". Despite the fact the court action involved federal jurisdiction over Indians and their land and over a number of other matters, such as migratory birds, fisheries and navigable waters, this government failed to take action.
The 1912 Quebec Boundaries Extension Act clearly defined the role of the federal government, providing in Section 2(c):
That the province of Quebec will recognize the rights of the Indian inhabitants in the territory above described to the same extent, and will obtain surrenders of such rights in the same manner, as the Government of Canada has heretofore recognized such rights and has obtained surrender thereof, and the said province shall bear and satisfy all charges and expenditure in connection with or arising out of such surrenders;
(d)	That no such surrender shall be made or obtained except with the approval
of the Governor in Council;
(e)	That the trusteeship of the Indians in the said territory, and the management of any lands now or hereafter reserved for their use, shall remain in the
Government of Canada subject to the control of Parliament.
The intent of the act is specific and clearly states that the "trusteeship of the Indians in the territory" shall remain with the federal government. How did this federal Liberal government respond to its constitutional and trust responsibilities? In
James Bay Agreement
July of 1971 a resolution passed by the Indian chiefs of the James Bay area was sent to the then Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to stop the James Bay project. The result-no action. In the spring of 1972 legal action was introduced by the Indians concerned, and again the Indians sought help from the federal government to participate in the case. The result-again the necessary action was not taken.
The decision of the government was described by the minister on numerous occasions as one that demonstrated the federal government was not as paternalistic as it had been in the past. In an effort to cover up this infamous scandal in its dealings with native people, this government avoided the controversy and attempted to appease its conscience by providing some assistance for legal funds.
The government's acquiescence to become an observer rendered meaningless both the special trust responsibility of the government and the justification for federal rather than provincial or corporate jurisdiction in dealing with the problems related to native people.
Of the many lessons learned from the James Bay episode, one of the most important is that a trustee cannot have divided loyalties. We saw it in Quebec, and we see evidence of this recurring in the Yukon territory, the Northwest Territories, and with the Inuit Tapirasit. The actors may have been different leading up to the James Bay agreement. However, the end result of a conflict of interest has prejudiced the natives' hopes that this government will honour its special constitutional and trust responsibilities.
If tragedy was the earliest form of drama, then the next act, which includes the period leading to the signing of the agreement and the subsequent introduction of new principles to the agreement, would be analogous to the Greek drama of Aeschylus in which the fates pursue the main character to his eventual doom.
The native leaders were forced to confront a silent federal government, a Quebec government committed to a $16 billion plus political scheme, the federal and provincial bureaucracies, and the giant corporations determined to develop the north at any cost. The odds were unbelievably overwhelming. Imagine, if you can, the following scenario-the necessity of the native people to negotiate with a gun to their heads knowing that the $16 billion project would proceed unchecked with the threat of a unilateral settlement being imposed without involvement. Imagine if you can the necessity to negotiate in downtown Montreal confronted with unfamiliar pressures and an uncomfortable environment. Would it not have made sense for the instant southern experts to have carried out a reasonable part of the negotiations at Fort Chimo, Aupaluk or Povunanituk in the north, to name but a few communities? Imagine, if you can, the necessity to meet an imposed deadline of November 1, 1975, or face the prospects of an imposed settlement.
I vividly recall meeting with a responsible, concerned group of Inuit late in the evening, during the latter part of August

December 7, 1976
James Bay Agreement
1975, and with their interpreter. Their request, which we pursued in the House of Commons the following day on October 29, 1975, by way of Standing Order 43 and questions, was to have the period of negotiations extended one month. May I repeat it was a simple request: to extend the negotiations for a period of only one month, during which time the Inuit believed that they could complete the negotiations. And what was the minister's response? He refused to intercede and take action. This was not a contract negotiating an hourly rate for a two-year period, but an agreement which would alter the lives of a people and their children and children's children for all time. Is it any wonder the native people distrust this government and question its motives?
Imagine if you can the necessity to impart the. details of a massive legal document to the native people affected by the agreement, in a relatively short period. I read and studied the agreement and had difficulty in interpreting the implications of many sections. Is it not reasonable to conclude that if I experienced such difficulties, then the Cree in the James Bay area and the Inuit on the Arctic circle who had a limited number of documents and, more important, too little time, would be in the impossible position of trying to understand the full impact of the agreement? And to compound the impossible, the initial agreement was written in French, subsequently translated into English, and only at the last minute under pressure was the document translated into the language of the native people, and then in an abbreviated form. Yet this government has the audacity to refer to a just society and participatory democracy.
Imagine if you can the necessity to take a vote on the proposal by March 11, 1976, which the former minister, in a moment of generosity, conceded, knowing perfectly well the proposal would not be understood by the natives in the time allotted, and the task of carrying out such a vote in the middle of winter would be one of Herculean dimensions.
Imagine if you can a small group attempting to reach the coastal communities of Inukjuak, Povunanituk, Ivujivik, Arud-livik, Sugluk, Wakeman Bay, Koartac, Payne Bay, Aupaluk, Leaf Bay, Fort Chimo, George River, and Port Burwell during February and March, in a hostile climate with poor communications.
We know the mission was accomplished and a vote taken, the results of which were admitted to be a foregone conclusion. However, it should be noted that even in the remote settlements on the Arctic, insulated and unaware of the power struggle occurring in the south, communities such as Povunanituk, Sugluk and Inujiuk sensed the threat to their way of life and their future and many registered their protest by refusing to vote.
The agreement raises a number of serious political issues which this government has endorsed by signing the settlement and by the introduction of this legislation. The most-important issue with the greatest potential impact on native people across Canada is the decision to allow the Quebec government the right to mould the future of the native people on its own terms.

This is in direct violation of the constitutional responsibilities of the federal government.
On November 6, 1975, an article appeared in the Montreal Gazette describing certain features of the agreement. In that article the MNA for Mount Royal, John Ciacca, who served as the provincial government negotiator, stated:
In effect the agreement will have precedence over the federal Indian Act...
It is our end to create a new concept within the framework of a Quebec law- the establishment of a community lived in either by Cree or Inuit of their own choice but also accessible to the rest of the population.
My understanding of the agreement is in accord with his observations. This obviously violates the constitutional responsibilities of the federal government as outlined in Section 91 of the BNA Act which set out the exclusive legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada and gave rise to the Indian Act.
When the federal government signed the agreement, for unexplained reasons it felt justice was served by omitting some native groups in Quebec from the negotiations. Can the minister possibly explain why the Naskapi, faced with the same fate as other natives in the north, were not included in the final agreement?
The minister knew that the Naskapi were a nomadic group indigenous to the area, having followed the caribou herds for untold generations. The minister knew that his department had been involved in the past with relocation plans which have failed to resolve the social problems affecting the Naskapi. And yet this government refused to play a leading role as the trustee of the Naskapi to ensure the future of these native people was protected and included in the agreement.
Again I would like to ask the minister what steps he has taken to protect the rights of the Inuit at Port Burwell. As the minister knows, the Inuit at Port Burwell have interests outside Quebec, yet the agreement, as I understand it, extinguishes all rights including those outside the boundaries of Quebec. I can assure the minister we will expect a full explanation of the facts.
In reading the agreement it is apparent the ultimate success or failure of the settlement will depend in great measure on the good will, on the understanding of the native people and their aspirations and trust, by the non-native signatories. That has not happened. Again this federal Liberal government stood idly by adopting the strategic position of alert neutrality while events occurred during the pre- and post-signing period which jeopardized the rights of native people.
On September 29 of this year I had a lengthy meeting with the NQIA land negotiating team to discuss one small aspect of the agreement. Their mandate was to finalize the selection of category I and category II lands under which the terms of the agreement had to be completed within two years of the signing of the settlement, at which time Quebec can unilaterally impose a choice of category I and category II lands on the Inuit.
Negotiations had reached an impasse despite specific provisions under section 6 of the agreement enabling the Inuit to make application to Quebec for the revision of the category I
December 7, 1976

lands, to take into account the wildlife productivity of the land and the usability of such lands for harvesting.
The rules of the negotiations had suddenly changed. The province of Quebec misinterpreted the provisions of the agreement which established the criteria to be followed by both parties in land selection. The province of Quebec ignored the spirit and the letter of other provisions in the agreement which deal with procedures for the selection of Inuit land needed for the project and the added new criteria affecting the land selection process. I see you are looking at the clock, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
As I was saying just before the bells rang at 8.30, the settlement will depend in great measure on the understanding of native problems, on good will and on a great deal of trust on the part of non-native signatories. I had been establishing the fact that this understanding was lacking. I pointed out that the government of Quebec had gone beyond the scope of the established criteria to which I had referred. It had been indicated that potential future development will take precedence over the present agreement which clearly defines the importance of the wild life productivity of the land and the use of the land with regard to harvesting. Actually future development, despite the vagueness of the term and lack of supportive evidence, was being used as the selection criteria. The province was insisting on new land selection criteria and that any final agreement must be a package deal. There was no final agreement even in the case of those communities which had entered into some form of agreement, and the threat that these communities would lose what little land had been agreed on was used as a negotiating device.
The position of the provincial government has ignored the fact that land selections are made on the merits of individual community circumstances since category 1 and category 11 lands must meet community and harvesting needs in specific geographic areas. I firmly believe that every member in the House, including the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Allmand), would privately concede, if they reviewed the history of category 1 land selections for Aupaluk, Leaf Bay and Payne Bay, that the Inuit people in the Arctic settlements have been used as pawns by powerful interest groups. Yet this federal Liberal government has persisted with its policy of "alert neutrality."
The greatest injustice and unfortunate feature of the negotiations are that Hydro Quebec and its right and left arm, the James Bay Energy Corporation and the James Bay Development Corporation, have been the principal negotiators or, more appropriately, the principal adversaries throughout the negotiations. During the negotiations on Inuit land selections the province of Quebec indicated that no agreement could be

reached without the consent of Hydro Quebec. For its part Hydro Quebec has indicated it will not agree to any land selections unless the Inuit sign certain conditions completely beyond the provisions of the agreement. These conditions are to the effect that, and I quote:
The Inuit will never invoke social impact factors or effects of proposed future hydroelectric projects on the coast, Wastapaka, Payne, Leaf, Caniapiscau, Lanch, Whale and George Rivers, for the purpose of opposing or hindering these projects.
This position is in direct violation of the spirit and intent of the agreement and will undermine the future development of native people and destroy their culture and economies. A major land settlement will not succeed unless the native people have the opportunity to take their full and rightful place in Canadian society and to enrich that society through their participation.
It is not my intention to discuss the various sections of the agreement. However, I want to acknowledge and commend the native people and their leaders for many of the concessions they obtained, despite overwhelming odds negotiated in an environment emphasizing development and exploitation at any cost without a parallel commitment to the future of a people.
To those who have read and studied the agreement it is evident that the ultimate success or failure of the existing settlement will depend on the good will, a thorough understanding of native people and their aspirations, and complete trust on the part of the signatories. As I indicated previously these essential ingredients have not, and do not exist, on the basis of the past performance of the non-native signatories. I have no reason to believe these attitudes will change.
Sir, it must be emphasized that there is no universal formula as to the necessary ingredients in other major land settlements to be negotiated. With respect to those who hold the view that the James Bay settlement will set a precedent for future land settlements, let me indicate that they either do not understand the regional differences or are discarding the issue with indifference. In either event if such attitudes persist in future negotiations, the ultimate goal to have native people succeed in Canadian society is doomed to failure.
When the Supreme Court in its 1973 decision recognized that the Nishga had aboriginal title in the Nass Valley, there was no effort on its part to define the exact nature of their rights, how to evaluate the rights or to extinguish the rights. This fact has been exploited by extremists at both spectrums of the issue. But surely the questions that must be asked are obvious. Do we want a continuation of welfare for native people? Do we want a continuation of alienation, with its implications, between the native people and the non-native community, or are we prepared to provide through land settlements a basis for stronger native communities and a more positive relationship with other Canadians? We have the opportunity to achieve the latter to the mutual benefit of all Canadians.
James Bay Agreement
Of the numerous lessons to be learned from the many tragedies surrounding the James Bay settlement, perhaps the most important is the approach used to achieve a settlement. The federal government's abrogation of its constitutional responsibilities, the Quebec government's commitment to development and insensitivity to the native people, and the ever-present adversary role of powerful Crown corporations, are maglignant symptoms which must be avoided in future land settlements.
When one assesses the broad picture of what has occurred in northern Canada, it is obvious that the policies of the government have failed to produce a society in which we can expect to see a general improvement of the quality of life of the native people.
It is apparent, in assessing the attitudes of those involved in discussions related to comprehensive land settlements, there is a marked difference in the native and non-native perception of the issues. Among the non-natives there is a tendency to see solutions in terms of our own experiences and values, which invariably are translated into economic terms by the power structures in the south and the belief the native people should be like us.
What we have failed to recognize and accept is that the native view is real and logical to them, and that they may not accept our approach to life in total, and that economic independence and economic self sufficiency may be conceived in ways different from our traditional views.
This does not imply that the native person seeking to improve himself and the position of his people believes it is possible nor even sensible to return to the "good old days". The hardships experienced by the native people as described by Rene Fumaleau in his book "As Long as the Land Shall Last" is not the lifestyle envisaged by the vast majority of native people today.
It is also apparent, and I believe the vast majority of native people recognize and have demonstrated, they are not prepared to adopt a position which has a serious adverse impact on Canadians or to adopt a position which would undermine government authority in vital areas. They are, however, telling Canadians the present situation is unacceptable and destructive to their future, and they see no hope through the democratic process to change the course of economic, social and political development. They are telling government and Canadians that changes must be made. They are seeking meaningful participation.

speechtext:
An important component to the approach taken to achieve land settlements which has received considerable attention is the time frame necessary to arrive at a final agreement. The James Bay settlement has clearly demonstrated the injustice of negotiating the future lives of a people by placing a time limit on a complex agreement and by tying such negotiations to major developments.
I view with apprehension any approach that in effect states it is possible to negotiate a comprehensive complex land settlement by crossing all the t's and dotting all the i's during a time frame that is either specied or implied. Such an approach will contain rigidities which will prove unworkable at some later date and give rise to new frustrations and new problems. Such an approach will be disadvantageous to the native people, will impede responsible development, and the resultant tragedies in human terms will weigh heavily on the consciences of those suggesting such a formula.
In dealing with human beings one must recognize that change is a continuum; no Canadian, either native or nonnative, has the ability or wisdom to outline a master plan for the evolution of native people or indeed any people. It is therefore essential to strive for an agreement which is flexible to permit the positive evolution of the native people; an agreement which the Government of Canada must honour with scrupulous integrity.
In concluding, I want to emphasize that any approach to the resolution of native problems in our democratic society must be based on the fundamental principle that all Canadians will benefit by supporting the development of a pluralistic culture in which the culture of the native people, as indeed of other minorities, will have the oppotunity to grow and develop.
There is no instant remedy to correct native problems, and the necessary measures must be implemented over a period of time that will permit their adaptation to the natives' growth, development and aspirations.
During my travels across Canada which have brought me in contact with a large cross section of the native community, I have been impressed that responsible leadership exists and new leaders are continually emerging. They are restructuring their national psychology in the direction of greater responsibility for their own fates. The vast majority of native leaders are energetic, creative, and despite years of paternalistic oppression are abandoning the colonialistic rhetoric of an earlier era, are articulating the present and seeking involvement in the future. Their legitimate aspirations must not go unheeded.
I am convinced the social problems oppressing our native people can be alleviated, not by the continuation of paternalistic attitudes but through the efforts of people sharing values fundamental to all mankind, and by bringing people closer

together through the things that make them happier and provide them more spiritual freedom.
The future strength of our country must rest with the interdependence of minority groups, and this is only possible by saving all components.
We have experienced an era of paternalism, we have seen the introduction of programs to rationalize our national guilt which has produced moral harm with its tragic consequences. It is the native people who have sacrificed their culture, traditions, and youth through their total dependency on the state. We have experienced the tragedies of economic development without a paralleled development of people.
Hydro Quebec, the James Bay Energy Corporation, and the James Bay Development Corporation are not the government of Quebec, are not the Government of Canada, and do not represent the will of the people. There is no evidence from their record that social impact is an integral part of their policies. By staying in the background and allowing the native people to negotiate their birthright with Crown corporations, both the federal and provincial governments have committed an unpardonable offence.

speechtext: By their silence they have condemned the native people to the whim of giant corporations, and this federal government has abrogated its constitutional and trust responsibilities on behalf of native people. As I indicated previously, there is no rapid or universal solution to their social problems; however, we must move with boldness, consistency, patience, and tolerance if we are to succeed. The federal government has failed on all four counts in introducing this legislation. It has lost the confidence of the native people of Canada. It has lost the confidence of minority groups in Canada who share the common aspiration of social justice. It has lost the confidence of all Canadians who place a value on people. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy indeed to make a few comments on the second reading of Bill C-9, a bill which I am sorry to say I will not be able to support as it now stands. I cannot support it for the very basic reason that the main purpose of the bill is the extinguishment for all time of native claims, rights, title and interests, whatever they may be, in and to the territory, of all Indians and all Inuit, wherever they may be, and all the native claims, rights, title and interests, whatever they may be, in Canada, of all the Inuit of Port Burwell. I am paraphrasing clause 3 of Bill C-9.
I have personally been involved for many years in at times the very lonely and difficult struggle to have native rights in this country of ours recognized and dealt with justly. I know what it is like, Mr. Speaker, to be out in the bush trying to
December 7, 1976

make a living as a hunter-trapper. I know what it is like to be hungry, when you are not sure where your next meal is coming from. 1 know what it is like to try to compete in the white man's world with very limited formal education. I can remember wondering, three or four days before payday, where my next meal was coming from. I had nowhere to stay, being too proud to ask my neighbour.
At the same time, Mr. Speaker, I tried to get the native people organized, whether in the Northwest Territories, the Mackenzie delta or Great Slave Lake. You try to raise funds from people, and get the general public to understand what it is like to try to compete in the white man's world. You try to get the rest of Canada and the world to recognize that the native people of this country have certain aboriginal, or legal, or whatever term you want to use, rights which they have had since time immemorial, and it is a very hard struggle.
My grandfather was born and raised in Arctic Village and comes from Alaska. Today his children and grandchildren are watching colour television which is brought to them by satellite, but this has happened only recently. In the north you have people caught between the white man's culture and Indian culture, people who do not know where to fit in. You work hard and spend many long, lonely hours bringing the message of the people. You might get a little encouragement, but not very much. Not only among your own people but there are those in the white society who call you names, call you a self-appointed leader, or radical red power, or a guy who is trying to radicalize the young people of this country-that sort of thing. You do the best you can and work your way up to the highest court in the land, the House of Commons. But when you get here, Mr. Speaker, you find introduced into the House this piece of paper, this modern day treaty, which is no better than any of the other treaties that we have signed across the country. We know the suffering they have caused many native people. This is why I am very saddened indeed to see such a bill as this now being debated in the House.
I had hoped that during my time in the House I would see a better and fairer bill brought forward, one that would recognize and enshrine in the British North America Act native rights, aboriginal rights, or legal rights, which is the term the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) once used, for the benefit of the first and original citizens of this land.
Instead, Mr. Speaker, what we are debating here is a bill that does the exact opposite; it extinguishes for all time the rights of, in this case, the native people of James Bay. The James Bay agreement represents the surrender of Indian and Inuit rights. I am not absolutely certain whether the Metis will be losing out as a result of this bill, but one can rest assured, Mr. Speaker, that the bill will put them in a losing position as well.
This surrender of rights extends to a very large area which the people of James Bay have been occupying since time immemorial. The people are being given a small reserve of land and a sum of money which looks to me like a large welfare cheque. This is not what I would like to see. According to the bill, the native people in the James Bay area are being
James Bay Agreement
promised some kind of guarantee of exclusive hunting, fishing and trapping rights, and continuing use of soapstone and of the forests in that area. Some kind of guarantee that is, Mr. Speaker! These people have always had and made good use of these rights. According to some archeologists, native people all across this land have been making use of these rights for thousands and thousands of years. In effect, this bill is guaranteeing something which I do not believe can be guaranteed in the first place.
When we hear reports of arsenic poisoning in places like Yellowknife, Northwest Territories, of mercury pollution in the Grassy Narrows and White Dog reserves of northwestern Ontario-and a few days ago I raised a question in the House about mercury pollution in Arctic Bay, which is close to the north pole-how can a government give this kind of guarantee? For example, Mr. Speaker, even as negotiations were continuing in the drawing up of the James Bay agreement, the native people in the area could actually see a huge hydroelectric dam being built on their hunting grounds. Is that a guarantee of hunting rights? Huge areas of land that people had used and occupied for thousands of years were being flooded. Again I ask the question, what kind of guarantee is this?
Bill C-9 looks to me like a modern day treaty. The intent of the bill is pretty well the same as other treaties agreed upon between some native peoples of Canada and the government of this country many years ago. In this what I call modern day treaty the Canadian government agrees to pay $225 million to the native peoples of the James Bay area who may be in agreement with this bill, over the next 20 years. This is what an Indian will get for signing away his aboriginal rights forever, Mr. Speaker.
As many native people in other parts of the country have sadly learned, it has not always been to the benefit of the people who have signed these treaties. This cash settlement amounts to about $1,000 a year per person. In the early treaties, of course, the Canadian government, as we all know, paid at the rate of $5 per person per year. While the Canadian government may have taken into consideration such modern day phenomena as inflation, whether the government pays $5 or $1,000 the terms are still the same and are not for the betterment of the native people.
All through Canadian history when a native person signed away certain land rights it has usually been to his detriment. I should like to give some examples in the Northwest Territories where I come from. This is the area covered by Treaties Nos. 8 and 11 which were signed back in the late 1890's-actually I believe Treaty No. 11 was signed in 1921. As I understand it, these treaties turned over to the federal government certain mineral rights, or sub-surface rights as they are called. This gave the government the authority to issue exploration and mining permits, prospecting permits and so on in connection with the search for and extraction of non-renewable natural resources such as gas, oil, gold and other minerals. As a result, the native peoples found they could not receive any royalties on major finds in the Northwest Territories.

December 7, 1976
James Bay Agreement
We did not fare very well in this area. For example, Norman Wells, an Imperial Oil Company town, has been operating for almost 40 years but we did not get many benefits from that operation. As a matter of fact, as far as I know only one northern native person has a full-time job at that site at the present time. I might mention the Pointed Mountain Gas Well near Fort Liard, a gas pipeline now in operation. We did not get one full time-job out of that project.
Neither did the native peoples of the territories get many benefits from such operations as the large lead zinc mine at Pine Point, two gold mines at Yellowknife, the tungsten mine near the Yukon border, or the Echo Bay mine on Great Bear Lake. I believe that had the treaties covering that area not been signed, and had the Dene been able to hold on to their aboriginal and native claims we would have at least been able to get some royalties in respect of the minerals which are now being exploited instead of all those royalties going directly to the federal government. In other words, if the native peoples of that part of Canada had retained their aboriginal rights, as common dignity says we should have been allowed to do, the Indian people would have enjoyed the royalties which resulted from technical development affecting their communities. We did not even get jobs, Mr. Speaker. At the beginning, that is, at the stage when the bush was being cleared, we did get some part-time work. But after the operations began we found ourselves in the cold.
All these treaties say the Canadian government would guarantee the hunting and trapping rights of the native peoples in the lands they have occupied. I believe that in the negotiation of these treaties it has been customary to use such terms as "As long as the rivers will flow, the grass will grow and the sun will rise ..hunting and trapping rights were to be protected. Yet we all know this is not happening. The Canadian government knows that these promises are hollow even as it makes them.
What can the Canadian government guarantee when we see the waters in Yellowknife Bay are polluted by arsenic so that the fish are no longer safe to eat? The people of the White Dog and Grassy Narrows reserves in northern Ontario know how hollow these guarantees are when they are told they should not eat the fish from the water system in the area because they are contaminated with mercury poison.
I feel that no hon. member of this House would honestly wish to be party to an agreement which extinguished the aboriginal rights of the native peoples for all time. What would the children of these people, and their children for that matter, say of us parliamentarians if we agreed in 1976 to the extinguishment of their aboriginal rights in the lands they have occupied since time immemorial? When will the government learn from previous experiences of such treaties? I would not like to be blamed for agreeing to a treaty with the people of James Bay under such intensive pressure.
I have referred to the treaties which were made earlier this century covering parts of the Northwest Territories. While I am on the subject of the Northwest Territories I might say
[Mr. Firth.)
that some months ago I asked the previous minister of Indian affairs a question about the James Bay settlement, as it is now called-whether it will be used as a precedent for other claims such as those which may be coming forward soon from the people of the Northwest Territories. I was not able to get an answer. The previous minister was not able to tell me how the Metis would fare either. As far as I know they are not even mentioned in this agreement. I have not studied the agreement in its entirety, but I asked the minister the following question on November 18, 1974:
Have the interests of Metis and non-status people in Northern Quebec been protected under the terms of the announced settlement?
The former minister replied:
I believe there are, roughly 200 non-status people involved in the area concerned in northern Quebec.
That answer does not tell me anything at all, Mr. Speaker. I asked him also whether this settlement would be used as a model for possible settlements affecting the Northwest Territories, and once again he gave me a non-answer. In fact though, this James Bay settlement does take in the Northwest Territories since it is mentioned that among the rights of the native people which are to be extinguished are included those of the Inuit of Port Burwell. And Port Burwell happens to be in the Northwest Territories. So I had to wait a couple of years before finding the answer to my question in this bill.
As I say, I would not like to be blamed for agreeing to such a treaty negotiated with the people of James Bay under such intensive pressure-The people were under extreme pressure to settle since many of them were afraid that if they did not they would be excluded from any of the benefits of the development which is taking place.
I should also like to mention the section which deals with the extinguishing of claims. I should like to see it completely removed from the bill. I believe it is in clause 3(3) of Bill C-9. This clause goes against the wishes of many people who are involved in the cause of fighting, working and struggling for the recognition and acceptance of the fact that the native people of this country have their basic aboriginal rights, and many of us believe that these rights should be enshrined in the BNA Act. It seems to me that the Canadian government does recognize that the native people have such rights by the very fact that this bill is attempting to extinguish those rights. Otherwise, why would this clause be in Bill C-9?
Goodness knows, the native people of this country have paid for these rights many times over. We have paid for them since the days of the first explorers who came to this land from across the sea. The first traders and the missionaries, as well as the government people, would not have survived in this country had it not been for the native people who welcomed them here and showed them this country. The native people have paid for these rights in many ways. They did not pay for them only with the birch bark canoe, the snowshoe or the lacrosse. The North American pharmaceutical society admits today that
December 7, 1976

there are over 400 drugs and remedies sold on the market that were originally used by the native people of this country.
The native people have paid, and paid again, with the loss of their culture, the loss of language, and the loss of their lives. They have paid with the loss of the beautiful lands across this country. They have paid by serving in the two or three wars in which our country has been involved. For example, they have served as communicators in the European countries where you could have heard some soldiers talking to each other in the Cree language. That is a pretty hard code for any European to break! We have served in many ways and we have paid for our rights.
We hear references to Canadian sovereignty. You send a few Mounties up north to fly a flag and you call that maintaining Canada's sovereignty! That is not the way to prove the sovereignty of Canada. The way to do it is to accept being a Canadian citizen by going up there and living up north, by building your home there, bringing up your family and making a livelihood off the land. That is maintaining sovereignty for Canada up north, and the Inuit have been doing this for thousands of years.
I say that our aboriginal, native, or legal rights have been paid for very dearly by many of my people. Let us take as an example Sir Alexander Mackenzie, a chap who went down the Mackenzie river, the mighty river which bears his name. According to the history books from which many of our children learn the history of Canada, Sir Alexander Mackenzie, the Scotsman who discovered the Mackenzie river, was quite a hero. But in fact it was not he who discovered the river. A group of Chippewa Indians took Mackenzie's group down that river in birch bark canoes, kept them warm, kept them fed, showed them the way down the river, and brought them back. Yet the history books say he discovered the Mackenzie river! There are many other examples.
One day the history books in this country should be corrected so that we will know the true history of the country, and then we will be a little more proud of the people who were the original citizens of this country. Now Bill C-9 wants to take away and extinguish the rights of the native people forever.
Only a few years ago when I was a little boy at home in Fort McPherson, the game officer, the fur trader, the missionary, or whoever else wanted to go into the bush did not go there by himself; he had to have a guide. There was a tragic occurrence when a group of Northwest Territories Mounted Policemen organized a patrol from Fort McPherson, the village where I was born and raised. They wanted to take a trip across the mountains. The Indian people had taken them over and back many times before. There was no problem, they thought. But when they tried it once by themselves, not one of the boys made it back. They are all buried at Fort McPherson.
Canada, this country, has always treasured its rights and freedoms, so it should not be acting in a negative way by trying to do away with the basic rights of many of its inhabitants. But this is what this bill is attempting to do. I believe that the Canadian government has a basic human obligation to
James Bay Agreement
provide general public services for the people of James Bay without asking them to sign away their aboriginal rights.
The minister mentioned the many goodies that are contained in this bill, the many good things that are in the bill for the people in the James Bay area. I think that is fine. It should have happened a long time ago. I myself do not live in the James Bay area. It is time that the government did what it could to improve its general image by bringing about justice and righting some of the wrongs that have been done to the James Bay people, and by looking after the general welfare of the native people all across this country.
I say that you have a good program for the James Bay people, but I do not believe these people want to sign away their rights as you go ahead with programs for economic development in the area. There are many plans for the area such as, as the minister mentioned, a police force manned by the Inuit or Cree in that area. That is great. Such are the plans for the James Bay area today, and the rest of the reserves will be looked after tomorrow. It is about time the government took upon itself responsibility not only for James Bay but also for other parts of the country.
