subtopic: JAMES BAY AND NORTHERN QUEBEC NATIVE CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO GIVE EFFECT TO AGREEMENTS WITH NATIVES OF NORTHERN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel privileged to follow the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth) in speaking on Bill C-9. I would like to thank you, Mr. Speaker, for giving me the opportunity to rise at second reading of this bill.
This legislation is to approve, give effect to and declare valid the James Bay and northern Quebec agreement and to protect, safeguard and maintain the rights and obligations contained in that agreement. I was happy to hear the hon. member for Northwest Territories mention the word "treaty" because in fact that is what this is. It just so happens that "agreement" is a word which has been put into Bill C-9. It took 102 years to make this transition. Now we are talking about an agreement, but in actual fact it is a treaty. If we were to take the time to read the treaties which were signed in Manitoba, and especially Treaty No. 5, we would find that the parallels are about the same.
This agreement has been the subject of much criticism and much apprehension, particularly on the part of Canada's aboriginal people. I feel that their criticisms and apprehensions are justifiable.
With regard to this issue I think it is time the government addressed itself to a very basic but very fundamental question. My understanding is that the BNA Act explicitly bestows legislative jurisdiction over Indians and their lands on the federal parliament and implicitly recognizes an obligation on the part of the federal government to protect the rights and interests of Indian people. In discharging this responsibility is the government not abrogating its legal responsibility to the Indians and Inuit of James Bay and northern Quebec by being a party to this agreement? The basic premise upon which the agreement is based is the principle of extinguishment of all Indian rights. By this action does this government feel that it is acting in the best interests of the Indian and Inuit as a trustee of their rights? I fail to see how it can.
The land claims of aboriginal people are at stake here. When the James Bay and northern Quebec agreement was signed on November 11, 1975, the federal government hailed the agreement as a tremendous breakthrough in Indian policy and as a model for future agreements. Again we must ask the government if considering this agreement a precedent in set-

tling future aboriginal claims is wise? If the government seriously condones this direction, then clearly it is in conflict with the views of the large majority of the native people of Canada who view aboriginal rights as the right of an Indian tribe or band to use and occupy their traditional land. Aboriginal rights are not for sale; they must be preserved. Settlement of claims must be based on land and political authority over that land. Settlement must not be based on cash compensation and the extinguishment of rights. I would like to emphasize "the extinguishment of rights".
In the case of the James Bay agreement, compensation in the amount of $225 million tax-free sounds like a lot, but in fact this amount will be doled out over a period of 20 years. What lasting development projects can be undertaken on this basis? Further to this the agreement states that all money will be paid to special corporations established for the purpose of administering the funds. The native people are to have the majority on the boards, but the Canadian and Quebec governments will be represented for 10 years. I call that blatant paternalism. Sure, the James Bay Cree and Inuit agreed to this, but many Canadians are cognizant of the fact that they did so under the threat of governments that if they did not sign they would get nothing. In fact many native people are saying that the Indians and Inuit of James Bay are getting little more than what was already available to them.
Is giving the Indians and Inuit exclusive rights to parts of their own lands, compensation? Is giving the Indians and Inuit hunting and Fishing rights limited to specific areas, compensation? Is giving the Indians Indian police to enforce white men's laws, compensation? Is making Indian lands municipalities, compensation? I can tell hon. members that it certainly is not.
In recognition of the Royal proclamation of 1763, which clearly assumes the rights of Indian people, I call upon the government to change its direction in terms of settlements of aboriginal rights. By proceeding with the James Bay agreement, the injustice which will be done to the native population and their children, yet unborn, is one to be reckoned with.
As a member of parliament for the Churchill constituency in Manitoba I feel very strongly about the government's direction in compensating Indians for loss of land. A parallel can be drawn between what is happening in the James Bay area and what is happening in regard to the Churchill River and Nelson River diversion project in Manitoba. They both began as concerns for hydro development, and both disregarded the native people in the areas, although their communities would be seriously affected.
Governments boasted that comprehensive environmental assessments had been made and that there would be compensation for those who would be affected. In Manitoba a consulting firm was hired, because of basic questions raised by the Northern Flood Committee in Manitoba, to reassess the initial assessment of the Churchill diversion project.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it ten o'clock?
December 7, 1976

AIRPORTS-WATERVILLE, NOVA SCOTIA-STATUS OF REQUEST FOR IMPROVEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to participate in this adjournment debate on the question I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) on December 3 concerning the status of the Waterville airport. I am glad to see the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Roy) in his place. Knowing the generosity and experience of the hon. member, I am hoping that he will have some positive and constructive comments to make about the future development of the Waterville airport.
In the time allotted to me under this procedure I do not want to belabour the House at this late hour with all the positive aspects and the obvious merits of getting financial assistance to develop the Waterville airport, which is in the heart of Kings county. Kings county is in the heart of my riding and is really the king county of Nova Scotia in terms of agricultural development and educational development. The Acadia University is right in the centre of the county, and Acadia not only wins hockey and basketball championships, but just last week played for a football championship against a college team from Ontario called Western. For the first half Acadia almost beat them, but in the second half there were too many Mustangs in the field, and unfortunately Acadia did not quite come through. However, Acadia did show that Kings county is appropriately named. It is an integral part of the Annapolis Valley riding.
For a properly developed commercial airport Waterville has the base, and it was in existence for over 30 years under private ownership. Finally, several years ago, the municipality took over the ownership so that the municipality could make an application to the Department of Transport for much needed financial assistance.
I also believe that the economic and technical studies required by the Department of Transport have been carried out. I hope that the parliamentary secretary will stand in his place tonight and indicate when a firm announcement will be made on financial assistance to Waterville. I see the hon. member for South Western Nova (Miss Campbell) tiptoeing out because the moon is high and the hour is late. She is fully aware of the assistance granted to the Digby airport. Assistance has also been granted to the Greenfield airport on the south shore and to Port Hawkesbury. Because of the configuration of my province, Mr. Speaker, the smaller airports can expedite traffic and help the tourist industry.
Adjournment Debate
I know the hon. parliamentary secretary is an historian and knows about the expulsion of the Acadians in 1755. As an Acadian I know the area is very attractive and the tourist industry is very important to it. For these reasons, and many others, I hope the parliamentary secretary can tell us what firm plan the department has in mind.
I do not want to end on a sour note, Mr. Speaker, but we have watched the development of other types of airports in Canada, be they an attempted Pickering or Mirabel, and while they involve so many more millions they cast a little cloud on the type of thinking that goes into development plans. In this case, however, because of a very cogent brief the minister received from the Affiliated Annapolis Valley Board of Trade and other people he should not have any problem in planning for the airport. We do not have to worry about some of the white elephants that might have been erected around the country because this airport in Waterville, Kings County, in the heart of the Annapolis Valley, could not be classed as a white elephant but could become a new incentive for development in the valley.

PETRO-CANADA-POSSIBILITY OF DISPOSING OF COMPANY TO PRIVATE ENTERPRISE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to participate in the adjournment debate because of the answer I received from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to a question on November 2. The question was as follows:
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is to the Prime Minister. In view of the fact that the throne speech referred to the possibility of Crown corporations being returned to private industry, would Petro-Canada fall within that category?

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
December 7, 1976
Adjournment Debate
The Prime Minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member will return to the throne speech, he will see that the words he uses are not there.
I shall refer to the pertinent part of the Speech from the Throne and to some of the remarks of a former deputy minister of industry, trade and commerce. In his answer the Prime Minister suggested that the words I had used are not in the Speech from the Throne. I therefore wish to clarify the basis of my questions and my reasons for asking them, and I appreciate the opportunity to do so in the present debate. The part of the throne speech to which I referred in my question reads:
In a further effort to reduce the size of government as well as expand the range of opportunities for private enterprise, all federal programs will be reviewed to identify those government activities which could be transferred to the private sector without reducing the quality of service to the public.
I agree that the words "Crown corporations" are not specifically mentioned, but if Petro-Canada is not a federal program which could be transferred to the private sector without reducing the quality of service, if it is not a program which does merit investigation, I can only wonder which programs can be transferred. If that sentence in the throne speech does not include Crown corporations, what does it mean?
The Canada Development Corporation was set up to be run as a business and ultimately, the majority of its shares were to be owned by the public. Petro-Canada was established without any specified goal with wide powers authorizing it to do almost anything; but apparently it does not necessarily work for financial gain.
I would like to quote what a former deputy minister of industry, trade and commerce, said at the Calgary energy conference last month. He said in part:
When one looks at Panarctic and Syncrude, it is somewhat reassuring that the government is in partnership with private companies which in each instance hold the controlling shares. There is reason to expect, therefore, that these ventures will operate on a business basis with a minimum of political interference. There is no such safeguard in the structure of Petro-Canada.
When Petro-Canada purchased Atlantic Richfield in Canada at a cost of $340 million, one more private industry was taken over by this government. If that corporation also buys Panarctic Gas at the mentioned price of $80 million, can we expect private companies to maintain a high level of incentive?
Where is this corporation headed? What will it do for Canadians? When will the powers given to this government under the act be explained, and how will those powers be limited? How can anyone say that Petro-Canada, regardless of the good intentions of its president, is being operated in the best interests of and for the expansion of opportunities for private enterprise?
Petro-Canada is merely duplicating, without restriction or guidelines, the services and functions of the CDC. Why not pour a fraction of those millions into the CDC instead of paying such unlimited amounts into a corporation which does not show any benefits, profits, advantages or encouragement for private industry? Are Crown corporations not part of this
[Mr. Towers.J
government? Anyone who is interested in industrial progress in this country would not seek to belittle a serious, legitimate question such as I asked on November 2.
Allow me to quote again from the speech which the former deputy minister made in Calgary. He said in part:
The private enterprise system can be destroyed just as easily by carelessness as by design. It is careless, to put it charitably, to launch state institutions into the realm of business where there is no vacuum to be filled and no clear purpose to be achieved.
It is equally careless to put forward a set of northern oil and gas regulations designed in part to give important preferences to the state enterprise over private enterprise, and in part to promote a show of economic nationalism by imposing a level of Canadian ownership large enough to discourage the multinationals in the industry and too small to mean anything in terms of Canadian control of any project.
Please note the following words spoken by the former deputy minister:
In the recent Speech from the Throne, the government indicated its intention of reviewing all federal programs for the purpose of identifying those activities that could be transferred to the private sector without reducing the quality of service. I suggest that Petro-Canada should be the first and foremost candidate for that review.
The recent report of the Auditor General criticized Crown corporations over which the federal government has jurisdiction. In all, the Auditor General was highly critical of lack of financial control in 21 Crown corporations. I suggest you can include Petro-Canada in that list of Crown corporations with respect to which the Auditor General is critical, because the Auditor General of Canada is the auditor of Petro-Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice Dupras (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while we may be tempted to agree with the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) with regard to the economy being better off within the private sector, in this case we are not speaking of a common business but of a non-renewable natural resource.
Notwithstanding the statement of a former public servant, which was referred to by the hon. member, the purpose of this Crown company is clearly spelled out in this legislation. I will again endeavour to impress upon the hon. member the aim of the legislation. It was, and I quote:
-to explore for hydrocarbon desposits, to negotiate for and acquire petroleum and petroleum products from abroad to assure a continuity of supply for the needs of Canada, to develop and exploit deposits of hydrocarbons within and without Canada in the interests of Canada, to carry out research and development projects in relation to hydrocarbons and other fuels, and to engage in exploration for, and the production, distribution, refining and marketing of, fuels.
The powers and duties of the corporation are defined with certainty in the act. Its board of directors, including highly qualified people from the private sector and three deputy ministers, ensures that the corporate performance is in accordance with the intention of the legislation. Company officers are of the highest calibre, and we have every confidence in them and are pleased with the initiatives they have already taken in the short history of the corporation.
I would like to remind hon. members of some of the reasons for the establishment of a national petroleum company. First,
December 7, 1976

while Canada has continued to be well served by industry, government by virtue of its responsibilities puts a higher value on having full knowledge of the Canadian resource base than the private sector can be expected to do. Public confidence in the long term adequacy of energy supplies is also of greater concern to the government.
Secondly, the strong role of government in the oil producing countries of the world, through the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), requires a government presence now in all countries having a heavy reliance on oil. Until Petro-Canada was established, Canada was behind most industrial countries in terms of a government presence in the industry.
Thirdly, Petro-Canada provides a window on the industry, which enables government to perceive industry problems and opportunities more accurately and, consequently, the company is of benefit to both the public and the private sector.
In summary, the compelling reasons for creation of a national petroleum company relate primarily to security of supply from domestic resources and also, as required, from abroad. Besides providing a new focus for mobilizing capital and skills in the service of necessary resource development, the company will bring to Canadians a sense of pride, satisfaction, and confidence in owning a portion of this criticially important Canadian industry.
I invite the hon. member to read the comments made by his colleague, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), on November 5, 1973, as reported at pages 7542 and 7543 of Hansard.

COMMUNICATIONS-PROVISION IN AGREEMENT WITH MANITOBA FOR EXTENSION OF CABLE TO RURAL AREAS- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 16 I asked the Minister of Communications (Mrs. Sauve) to spell out specific details on the agreement that had been signed between the Manitoba government, owners of Manitoba Telephone System, and the Canadian government, specifically its Department of Communications, in which the Department of Communications and the Manitoba government negotiated an agreement whereby the Manitoba government would be in control of the hardware for all cablevision in Manitoba.
At that time, as reported at page 1042 of Hansard I indicated to the minister that a monopoly had been granted to the Manitoba government through its public utility, Manitoba Telephone System, and that up to that date we had not received the extension of cable television in rural areas for which we had asked some two years previously. The minister then said:
Mr. Speaker, as far as I know the CRTC is on schedule as to the examination of applications for cable.
Adjournment Debate
I then said:
No. Two years.
The minister continued:
No, sir. They are on schedule. They come down with their decisions and I have nothing to do with the decisions of the CRTC as they apply to specific applications.
What is the case? The case is simply this, Mr. Speaker. Hearings were held on May 17, 1974, in Winnipeg, which are quoted in the Winnipeg Free Press of the same date. I quote the following:
A Winnipeg cable television firm outlined Thursday an $8.6 million plan to transmit its programs to 31 rural Manitoba communities on a microwave system that it wants to build.
The article then went on to list some 31 communities in rural Manitoba to which this cable company wanted to extend cablevision.
What happened then? We find out very clearly that the Manitoba Telephone System was really not interested in the extension of cablevision to rural Manitoba. The reason I say that is this. To quote the same article of May 17:
Mr. Mitchell-
He was with CKY-TV.
-said that his company would like to begin immediately to extend CKY-TV to the Arborg area, followed later by service to Flin Flon, Snow Lake, The Pas and Thompson.
During his presentation Mr. Mitchell told commission members his firm was experiencing many frustrations in its attempt to arrange for microwave transmission facilities to get its signals to Dauphin.
He said both the Manitoba Telephone System and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation have demanded excessive rates and his firm cannot get permission to erect its own facilities in Riding Mountain National Park.
The point I am trying to make is that the record of Manitoba Telephone System in providing the hardware for the extension of cable television into rural Manitoba is simply abominable. What has happened now is that the Department of Communications, which is supposed to protect viewer rights to receive cable television in the same way as people in urban areas, has now given the Manitoba Telephone System the monopoly not only of deciding where cable will go, but they now control the total hardware. This simply means that the Manitoba Telephone System has complete control.
The minister said that the CRTC was up to date on its decisions. What has happened since the May 17, 1974, hearing, more than two years ago? A decision was made with tremendous alacrity. The decision was announced again in the same paper on July 5, 1974, a month and a half after the hearings, which allowed Winnipeg Videon Limited to amend its cable television broadcasting licence for part of Winnipeg, Manitoba, to add a new remote head end antenna site near Tolstoi, Manitoba. That head end antenna site is in my riding, down in the very southern part of the riding. The purpose of the application to extend the head end antenna was to extend the cable television into rural Manitoba.
They got a licence from the CRTC for the head end antenna, but that is just half the decision. There the minister was quite right. But since that date the CRTC has made no

December 7, 1976
Adjournment Debate
decision on the extension of cable television into rural Manitoba, so I would ask the parliamentary secretary, what does the minister mean by saying that on the one hand they are up to date on decisions, yet two years later we are still waiting? Or is two years "up to date"?
The hassle that has gone on between the federal government and the provinces as to who controls communications has victimized rural people. They want the same cable television viewing rights as people in urban areas. I say to the parliamentary secretary he should forget about his prepared notes and tell us exactly what the government is going to do on this issue. In other words, what guarantees have been given by the Manitoba Telephone System, the public utility of the Manitoba government, that it will extend cable television into rural Manitoba? In a presentation to members from Manitoba they indicated that the microwave system is going right through our ridings and that it can be done at any time.
Has the Department of Communications asked the Manitoba system when the extensions will take place? When will the CRTC make decisions on applications made two years ago for the extension of cablevision into rural Manitoba? Lastly, what guarantee has the government or the department given to the people of Canada, and especially of Manitoba, that the Manitoba Telephone System should not only control the hardware but should now be on the production end as well? I do not believe government should be in that type of industry.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Milne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subtopic: COMMUNICATIONS-PROVISION IN AGREEMENT WITH MANITOBA FOR EXTENSION OF CABLE TO RURAL AREAS- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the pleasure to answer the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp).

No one has more desire to see cable television extended to rural residents than has the parliamentary secretary. Having
been born and raised in a rural area, he is certainly aware of the limited communications facilities which many Canadians in rural areas have found available to them in the past.
I wish to point out to the hon. member opposite that article IX of the agreement does recognize that the CRTC will continue to determine the timing and conditions for the introduction of cable television, that is, programming services, into the various locations in Manitoba. Furthermore, under article VIII, the provincial government has committed the Manitoba Telephone System to readily make available sufficient telecommunications capacity to permit the distribution of all federally authorized cable t.v. services.
I believe it is clear that one of the prime motivations of the provincial governments in seeking this agreement was precisely to ensure that coaxial cable systems should be developed on a rational and economical basis throughout Manitoba, and not be limited to the major urban areas as is the case in most other provinces.
The two governments agree to co-operate to ensure the orderly extension of service, both CATV programming and other telecommunication services. It would be my view that concluding this agreement should expedite the extension of services. The negotiation and agreement of related considerations might perhaps have been a problem in terms of holding up some of the extension work while the jurisdictional question was being worked out, but I would expect now that in the spirit in which the agreement was concluded an extension of cable services to the rural residents will result. Here again a great deal rests with the province and its relationship with the Manitoba Telephone Service.
